papers.title: Safety and Resilience in Slope Engineering Design for New Buildings under Extreme Rainstorm Climates
papers.summary: The safety of construction slopes holds significant importance in engineering and architecture, with the lack of resilience against extreme weather conditions being particularly critical. This paper systematically examines the fundamental flaws in traditional design theories regarding the limitations of compression-shear stress paths and the assumption of constant soil parameters. It delves into the systemic vulnerabilities in resilience across the entire lifecycle caused by operational supervision gaps and post-event regulatory gaps in the current construction system. Additionally, it reveals the consequences of mechanistic isolation between structural support and ecological protection, as well as the oversimplified engineering approach resulting from outdated drainage system standards, through real-world disaster case studies. Based on this, this article proposes a theoretical revision direction for constructing a tension shear fluid-solid coupling unsaturated soil mechanics system, explores a differentiated zoning control mechanism based on quantitative risk analysis (QRA), and integrates digital Bayesian pre-evaluation methods with on-site observations. The research aims to provide rigorous theoretical support for the disaster-resistant design of high-risk building slope engineering, and promote the transformation of slope engineering from static defense to a dynamic resilience management paradigm throughout its lifecycle.

papers.title: Integrating rockfall and debris flow monitoring and early warning networks into risk mitigation and emergency planning in Brescia Province, Italy
papers.summary: Italy is highly exposed to rapid landslides such as rockfalls and debris flows, which strongly affect mountain communities, infrastructure, and land management. Mitigation strategies traditionally rely on structural measures, including active stabilization works and passive protection systems, but their effectiveness depends on site-specific geological and geomorphological conditions and event magnitude. In this context, monitoring and Early Warning Systems are increasingly recognized as essential tools to complement structural interventions and reduce loss of life. Recent advances in sensors, communication technologies, and data processing have made local and territorial landslide Early Warning Systems more feasible, although their implementation remains challenging due to false alarms, threshold definition, validation procedures, and the need for continuous maintenance. This paper presents three case studies from the Province of Brescia, Northern Italy, showing how monitoring and alarm systems can be integrated into risk mitigation and land management. The first concerns a rockfall-prone site where unusual trajectories and high bounce heights required a combined system of flexible barriers, a multipurpose interception net, impact sensors, and traffic-light-based warning devices. The second describes a debris-flow Early Warning Network based on continuous meteorological and hydrometric monitoring, event-triggered wire sensors, and rainfall thresholds. The third illustrates an integrated multi-hazard network that monitors rockfalls, debris flows, and floods at the municipal scale. Together, the case studies highlight the value of combining structural and non-structural measures to support emergency planning and improve territorial safety.

papers.title: Neural network derived landslide risk assessment system
papers.source: Journal of Environmental Engineering and Landscape Management
papers.summary: Landslide is a frequent form of natural disaster in a tropical region such as Western Sarawak, Malaysia, and the occurrences are commonly associated with the wet season. Contemporarily, Landslide Susceptibility Map (LSM) produced by machine learning models are used to assess the landslide risk. However, LSMs are known to have spatiotemporal issues, where recent changes in the spatial data used as inputs in the models are not reflected in the LSMs, causing unjustified landslide susceptibility score in certain areas. The same issue was also observed in Western Sarawak’s LSM. Thus, this study was focused on transforming the Artificial Neural Network model used developed the region’s LSM into a set of equations that can be used as a landslide risk assessment system. The new system was determined to be highly accurate with a score of 1 for both Area Under the Curve score, and recall.

papers.title: A multi-source EO Framework for assessing permafrost thawing impact on land degradation in the Arctic region
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: EarthTrends is a multi-source Earth Observation framework developed to assess the impact of permafrost thaw on land degradation across the Arctic. Rapid warming is accelerating processes such as thermokarst formation, vegetation change, slope instability, and risks to infrastructure, yet monitoring these dynamics requires integrating heterogeneous satellite datasets and analytical methods. EarthTrends addresses this challenge through a modular Python architecture that fuses long-term satellite archives (Landsat), Copernicus Sentinel data, MODIS time series, and high-resolution optical imagery with advanced statistical and artificial intelligence approaches. The framework quantifies ecosystem change using multi-sensor vegetation index time series analysed through linear regression, Mann–Kendall trend tests, and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) models to detect non-linear dynamics and anomalies. Thermokarst features are automatically mapped from high-resolution imagery using a U-Net deep learning segmentation model. Land degradation susceptibility is further evaluated by modelling soil freeze–thaw cycles as proxies for slope instability and landslide potential. Environmental indicators are intersected with socio-economic datasets to estimate impacts on settlements and infrastructure. Preliminary results show that the thermokarst detection component is operational and capable of identifying surface subsidence features, while freeze–thaw analyses reveal anomalies linked to areas of increased degradation risk. Vegetation trends highlight spatially heterogeneous ecosystem responses to warming across the Arctic. Overall, EarthTrends demonstrates the feasibility of an integrated, scalable framework for monitoring permafrost-driven environmental change and its societal implications. The system is intended for pan-Arctic application and will be released as an open-source tool to support research, monitoring, and decision-making related to climate-induced land degradation.

GIS-based assessment of population and dwelling exposure to landslide-prone areas in the Valencian Community (Spain)
papers.summary: The spatial identification of population exposure to landslide-prone areas is essential for risk-informed territorial planning, particularly where impacts affect peri-urban and dispersed residential areas rather than consolidated urban centres. This study presents a GIS-based, multi-scale methodology to quantify and locate population and dwelling exposure beyond administrative boundaries by integrating landslide susceptibility mapping, residential cadastral data, and high-resolution population information from the 2021 census grid. Exposure is assessed by combining residential cadastral parcels with high- and very-high-susceptibility zones and aggregating exposed parcels into Residential Clusters at Risk (RCr). Exposure values are classified using Tail Quantiles Breaks (TQB) based on the P50, P70, P85, and P95 percentiles, providing a classification scheme well suited to heavy-tailed population distributions. Application to the Valencian Community (Spain) shows that population exposure is low at the regional scale (approximately 0.25% of the total population) but spatially uneven. Inland areas exhibit higher exposure intensity associated with permanent residential settlements, whereas coastal tourist-oriented areas concentrate higher absolute exposure linked to extensive built-up areas. Sensitivity analyses confirm the robustness of the methodology across aggregation radii and classification thresholds. The proposed methodology supports territorial planning and preventive interventions but represents an exposure assessment rather than a complete landslide risk analysis.

papers.title: Monitoring in Open-Pit Mines
papers.summary: Open-pit mining creates large, evolving excavations with high rock slopes, variable hydrogeological conditions, and continuous disturbance from blasting and excavation. These factors make slope instability a persistent operational risk and a major safety hazard. Modern open-pit geotechnical monitoring has therefore shifted from periodic, manual measurements to integrated, near-real-time systems that combine surface and subsurface sensors, ground-based radar, laser scanning, UAV photogrammetry, and satellite InSAR. In Mining 4.0, these sensing technologies are increasingly connected through IoT-enabled data acquisition, automated quality control, analytics pipelines, and decision-support tools, including digital twins and trigger-action response plans (TARPs), to provide timely warnings, reduce exposure to hazardous ground movement, and support production continuity. This chapter presents a practical framework for designing and operating slope monitoring programs in open pits, linking failure mechanisms to monitoring objectives, instrument selection, data management, alarm philosophy, and operational response. Several case studies illustrate how multi-source monitoring improves hazard recognition, forecasting, and risk-based decision-making, including the 2013 Manefay landslides at Bingham Canyon Mine and operational examples of radar, prism, UAV, and InSAR integration.

papers.title: GIS-based spatial prioritization of natural-hazard exposure and recorded COVID-19 case counts in Lemery, Batangas, Philippines
papers.summary: Local governments often maintain separate natural-hazard maps and health-surveillance records but lack a transparent method for identifying areas where these concerns overlap. This study applied a Geographic Information System (GIS) sieve-mapping approach to prioritize the 46 barangays of Lemery, Batangas, Philippines using 2,505 confirmed COVID-19 cases and ten natural-hazard layers covering seismic, landslide, coastal, flood, and volcanic hazards. QGIS was used to convert hazard classes into ordinal scores, adjust scores according to the proportion of barangay area affected, apply predefined weights, and generate a composite ranking. The decision premise was that barangays with high absolute COVID-19 case counts and substantial mapped hazard exposure may warrant greater preparedness priority. A balanced 50/50 weighting between the health and natural-hazard domains was used as an a priori screening scenario, not as evidence of equal contributions to disaster loss. Natural-hazard weights reflected qualitative local frequency information rather than probabilistic loss estimates. The additive combining rule summed the scaled health component and weighted, area-adjusted hazard scores without modelling interactions or joint probabilities. Bukal recorded the highest absolute number of confirmed COVID-19 cases, while District IV, Wawa Ibaba, Palanas, Mataas Na Bayan, and Sambal Ilaya received the five highest composite priority scores. The resulting ranking represents relative planning priority rather than infection risk or probabilistic disaster risk. Future work should incorporate population normalization, sensitivity analysis, vulnerability and exposure indicators, hazard interactions, and finer-resolution data.

papers.title: Flood and Landslide Risks in Border Regions
papers.summary: The increasing frequency of hydrometeorological disasters in border regions reflects the interaction between environmental degradation, land-use change, and climate variability. Nunukan Regency, as a strategic border area of Indonesia, faces significant development pressure due to the conversion of forests and agricultural land into plantations and settlements. This study examines how environmental degradation contributes to rising disaster risks and its relevance to spatial planning policy design. It focuses on the roles of land-use change and rainfall in shaping the spatial distribution of flood and landslide risks and their integration into the 2024–2043 Regional Spatial Plan (RTRW). Using a qualitative descriptive approach based on secondary data, the findings show that upstream land cover changes increase runoff and intensify flood risks downstream, while vegetation loss in hilly areas elevates landslide risks. Although the RTRW has incorporated disaster mitigation conceptually, gaps remain in aligning policy design with land-use control.

papers.title: Implementing a climate-resilient and inclusive WASH guidance in Indonesia: A mixed-methods case study.

Evidence remains limited on how WASH programs integrate climate resilience, equity, and social inclusion and on the conditions that enable benefits to reach households. Researchers examined how Climate Change Response for Inclusive WASH (CCRIW) guidance was implemented and adapted within routine programming in Indonesia, how implementation outcomes related to post-implementation household access, and which contextual factors enabled or constrained such access. Communities primarily adopted lower-cost actions aligned with immediate needs, available resources, and perceived feasibility. Household modifications supported more resilient and inclusive access but could not replace system-level investments under severe hazards. papers.title: Contrasting drivers of summer extreme hourly precipitation over the southeastern and northeastern Tibetan Plateau
papers.summary: Abstract Extreme hourly precipitation (EHP) across the Tibetan Plateau (TP) often triggers flash floods and landslides due to the region's complex and steep terrain, yet its inter-station covariations and formation mechanisms remain inadequately understood. Using climate network analysis of hourly station data and dynamic diagnostics, this study examines EHP synchronicity across the southeastern and northeastern TP and elucidates the underlying mechanisms from a perspective of sea surface temperature (SST)-forced circulation evolution. Results show weak inter-regional synchronization of EHP occurrence between the southeastern and northeastern TP, along with an insignificant correlation in EHP frequency (EHPF) between the two subregions, indicating largely independent governing physical processes. The southeastern TP EHPF is controlled by an upper-tropospheric South Asian anticyclone and a low-level anticyclone over the Arabian Sea. The South Asian anticyclone weakens after 2000, accompanied by intensified cyclonic circulation over the northern TP. In contrast, the northeastern TP EHPF is dominated by a quasi-barotropic Northeast Asian anticyclone throughout the entire period. SST drivers of EHPF over these two subregions exhibit both regional differences and interdecadal shifts. During 1979–1999, southeastern TP EHPF is linked to an eastern North Atlantic tripole SST anomaly pattern through a teleconnection wave train, whereas northeastern TP EHPF correlates with a western North Atlantic tripole configuration. After 2000, Eurasian Arctic SST anomalies emerge as dominant signals—a dipole pattern for the southeastern TP and a uniform warming pattern for the northeastern TP. These results underscore the need for region-specific EHP analysis and prediction strategies and highlight the growing role of the Arctic.

papers.title: Analysis on deformation and failure of multi-stage high slopes in open-pit mines based on strength reduction method
papers.summary: Multi-stage high slopes in open-pit mines containing weak diabase dikes exhibit complex progressive stepwise sliding failure under the combined effects of excavation disturbance and rainfall, yet their staged instability evolution laws remain insufficiently clarified in existing research. Taking the No.1 high slope of the Maoniup Rare Earth Mine in western Sichuan as the research object, this study systematically reveals the deformation-failure mechanism controlled by diabase weak interlayers through field geological investigation, in-situ shear tests and FLAC3D strength reduction numerical simulation. Field surveys show that the slope develops numerous tensile cracks on multi-level platforms and local slumping between platforms, with fractured, water-sensitive diabase dikes serving as the dominant internal weak structural planes triggering instability; Monitoring data show a progressive-failure pattern propagating from the 3,056 m platform toward the 3,080 m platform; in-situ shear test results confirm that diabase possesses extremely low saturated shear strength, which deteriorates sharply after rainwater softening. A three-dimensional numerical model matching actual stratigraphy and platform topography is established, and the Mohr–Coulomb strength reduction method is adopted to reproduce the whole progressive failure process under continuous strength degradation. The simulation results indicate that deformation initiates at diabase outcrops on the upper 3,056 m platform, and shear strain bands and plastic failure zones gradually extend downward along diabase belts to form interconnected through-going slip surfaces across multi-stage platforms, which well reproduces the field stepwise sliding characteristics. Numerical calculations using saturated geomechanical parameters under rainfall conditions yield a slope safety factor of 1.15, and the resultant deformation-failure pattern is highly consistent with simulation results obtained with strength reduction factors

papers.title: Residual shear strength of tropical granitic soils in Peninsular Malaysia
papers.summary: Introduction: Residual shear strength is an important parameter in the assessment of long-term slope stability and reactivated landslides. However, limited information is available on the residual shear strength behaviour of tropical granitic residual soils in Malaysia. This study investigated the residual shear strength characteristics of granitic residual soils collected from three locations in the northern region of Peninsular Malaysia: Kulim Hi-Tech, Bukit Suling, and Bukit Katak. Materials and methods: Laboratory characterisations encompassed physical index testing, particle density determination, mechanical sieve–hydrometer analyses, and Multiple-Reversal Direct Shear Testing (MR-DST) conducted under fully drained, saturated conditions across effective normal stresses of 50 kPa, 100 kPa, and 150 kPa. Results: The results indicated that residual shear behaviour was predominantly friction-controlled, with adopted effective residual friction angles ranging from 18.9° to 23.5°. Regression analysis revealed strong negative linear trends between effective residual friction angle and soil index properties (plasticity index (PI), liquid limit (LL), and clay fraction (CF)). However, because these relationships were derived from three site-level observations ( n = 3) without external validation, they are presented strictly as preliminary site-specific empirical correlations and must not be interpreted as design-ready predictive tools. Conclusions: This study expands the limited database for tropical granitic residual soils in Malaysia, demonstrating that index properties provide practical preliminary screening guidance while highlighting that direct, site-specific laboratory testing remains indispensable for final geotechnical design.

papers.title: Refinement of the Burridge and Knopoff Resistance Function with the Elementary Catastrophe Theory
papers.summary: The soil liquefaction occurs in water-saturated soils, involving a phase transition from solid to fluid when the soil loses strength and stiffness due to some change in its stress conditions. In physics, processes of this type are modeled according to the “fold” elementary catastrophe (for example, the over-saturated vapor condensation as well as some electromagnetism phenomena). Unlike our case, the respective graphs representing the aforementioned phenomena were obtained before the emergence of the Elementary Catastrophe Theory, which therein only clarified the processes and suggested some applications. In our circumstances, the behavior of the soil resistance at low speeds was not known. Consequently, after an appropriate application of the “fold” catastrophe, it was provided the resistance law at low speeds. All of the above would allow through the reengineering methods obtaining valuable information related to the structure and behavior of local plates. With this, we dared to suppose that in view of future landslide models already there is available a “standard” basic description that we believe is essential to be included at the time of any further development.

papers.title: Edukasi dan Sosialisasi Kebencanaan Longsor Berbasis Komunitas untuk Penguatan Kelembagaan Komunitas Peduli Lingkungan Kampung Asbaken
papers.summary: Kampung Asbaken in Distrik Makbon, Kabupaten Sorong, faces recurring landslide risks due to steep topography, high rainfall, uncontrolled land clearing, and sparse deep-rooted vegetation. Compounding this vulnerability, local disaster literacy is limited, and the partner group, Komunitas Peduli Lingkungan Kampung Asbaken, lacks formal organizational structures and standard operating procedures (SOPs). This community engagement initiative aimed to enhance community-based landslide mitigation and strengthen local institutional capacity through training, participatory risk mapping, slope bioengineering, and evacuation-route marking. Involving 25 partner members and 30 residents across three workshops, the program evaluated knowledge gains using a 30-item pretest-posttest instrument. The mean knowledge score increased by 78.6%, rising from 48.7 (SD = 9.8) to 87.0 (SD = 6.9), while passing rates (score ≥ 70) improved from 20.0% to 90.0% (paired t = 17.4, p < .001). The partner group also formalized its organizational structure and mitigation SOPs. These results show that participatory education integrated with vegetative conservation and institutional capacity building effectively enhances rural disaster resilience.

papers.title: Data and analysis code for: Behavioral evaluation of two roadside warning formats in immersive virtual reality for landslide-risk driving
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: This archive accompanies the article "Behavioral evaluation of two roadside warning formats in immersive virtual reality for landslide-risk driving" by Arjun Mehra, Kulbhushan Chand, Tad Gonsalves, Joachim Meyer, Akash K. Rao, K. V. Uday and Varun Dutt. It contains the de-identified data and the Python code needed to reproduce the statistics and Figures 3 and 4 reported in the article. Participants were randomly assigned to an active warning (an illuminated beacon) or a passive warning (a static landslide sign) and drove two attempts in a VR landslide scenario. Vehicle telemetry was logged throughout.

papers.title: An AI-Based Early Warning Framework for Natural Disasters in Afghanistan
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: Afghanistan gets hit by floods, earthquakes, landslides, droughts and avalanches, sometimes all in one year, sometimes in the same valley. In remote mountain villages the damage gets worse for a simple reason: the warning shows up late, or it never shows up. This paper sketches an early warning system built around Afghan conditions, with AI handling the data work. It would pull in weather readings, past disaster records, satellite images and terrain data, then estimate how likely each hazard is and sort that into four risk levels. Warnings would go out by SMS, radio, mobile apps and local community networks, but only after a real person has checked them.To be upfront, this is a proposal and nothing is running yet. Earthquakes can't be predicted, so for those the aim is risk maps and faster alerts once one has started. The idea is to back up the official disaster-management agencies and leave the final calls with them.

papers.title: Mass movements in the southern Black Forest, Germany
papers.summary: Despite their importance as geomorphological processes and natural hazards, systematic inventories of mass movements remain limited for many Central European mid-mountain ranges. This study presents an inventory map of mass movements in the southern Black Forest (Germany), on the area of the Late Pleistocene Feldberg glaciation. High-resolution digital elevation models combined with field surveys were used to map and classify mass movements. Potential preconditioning factors (aspect, slope angle, lithology) were analysed. In total, 158 mass movements were identified, affecting 36.2 km² (6%) of the study area. Slides dominate the inventory (36%). The spatial distribution reveals two clusters with higher frequencies, larger sizes and greater vertical extent of mass movements. Mass movements concentrate in gneiss, suggesting lithology as an important preconditioning factor, although topography also plays a role. The inventory provides a basis for future studies on slope failure chronology, glacial influence on landscape evolution and susceptibility assessment.

papers.title: The failure mechanism of moraine landslides induced by combined effect of freeze-thaw cycles and rainfall infiltration: Insight from the flume model test
GeoPhysAdapter: Scale-matched geophysical adaptation for cross-domain landslide mapping with vision foundation models
papers.source: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
papers.summary: Newly triggered landslides rarely carry immediate annotations, so cross-domain transferability determines the value of landslide mapping for emergency response and regional risk assessment. Vision foundation models have strengthened representational transfer, yet on unseen regions, events, and sources they still generate high-confidence false alarms. Terrain, material, and rainfall triggering can constrain such errors, but their supports are local, regional, and event-scale, so resampling onto a 10 m grid misaligns them with the segmentation decision unit and compounds the uncertain geographic context problem (UGCoP). We propose GeoPhysAdapter, which anchors on a frozen vision foundation model, restricts terrain, material, and triggering to dense spatial guidance, regional modulation, and event-timing forcing, and applies bounded adaptation at two decision units, the pixel and the candidate landslide body, reverting exactly to the visual prediction where support is insufficient. On an event-isolated PILD dataset of four public sources, 55 global landslide events, and 7890 test samples, 70.3% of cross-domain false-positive mass lies in near-pure spurious bodies of median equivalent diameter 207 m, matching coarse-prior support rather than the pixel. Pixel-level adaptation removes a net 507,817 erroneous pixels, reducing error by 7.76%, whereas raising the decision unit to the candidate body, under identical samples, anchor, and baseline, increases error reduction to 23.99% and improves IoU by a relative 14.2%. The gain decreases monotonically with terrain displacement, exceeds a strong optical control of spectral change and visual confidence alone by 0.019 IoU, remains positive across five vision anchors, and survives a pre-registered re-execution with a 20.61% error reduction. The binding constraint is therefore the match between the native scale of physical priors and the operative decision unit, not denser physical stacking. Data and code are publicly available at

papers.title: Synergistic effects of climatic drivers and anthropogenic land degradation on cascading geomorphic hazards in Iran
papers.summary: Environmental hazard adaptation frameworks have predominantly focused on susceptibility to isolated hazards, often overlooking the complex dynamics of cascading land degradation. This study assessed the synergistic impacts of anthropogenic and climatic drivers on cascading geomorphic hazards in Iran. Our framework integrated land degradation models (MEDALUS and RUSLE) with downscaled outputs from 23 General Circulation Models. We introduced the Dust Hotspot Severity Index (DHSI) utilizing a multi-threshold spatial intersection of Aerosol Optical Depth anomalies. Our analysis revealed hydro-aeolian telecoupling, in which upstream hydrological alterations drive downstream aeolian dynamics. Severe upstream soil erosion and the expansion of hydrological infrastructure have reduced environmental flows to downstream wetlands, triggering neo-playa formation. The subsequent accumulation of erodible sediments transforms desiccated wetland and lake beds- such as Lakes Urmia and Hamun- into hyper-productive dust sources (DHSI > 20%). Copula-based ensemble projections under the SSP2-4.5 scenario for the near-future period (2026–2050) indicate that desertification and water erosion rates will increase by 17.53% and 15.30%, respectively. The spatial extent of moderate-to-severe cascading hazard potential (encompassing desertification, water erosion, and dust emissions) is projected to expand from a historical baseline of 45.30% to 58.60%. These findings demonstrate how the convergence of unsustainable resource management and climatic drivers pushes arid landscapes toward cascading multi-hazard regimes.

papers.title: Integrated Physical Climate Risk Assessment for Energy Infrastructure Resilience and Adaptation
papers.source: SPE Asia Pacific Oil & Gas Conference and Exhibition (APOGCE)
papers.summary: Abstract As an energy industry, Pertamina faces climate risk consisting of transition risk and physical risk, where physical impacts increasingly influence asset integrity and operational reliability. This paper assesses physical climate risks to Pertamina operational assets across upstream exploration and production (E&P), refinery, and retail and distribution business units located in Southern Sumatra, Western Java, and Central Sulawesi. The scope focuses on identifying climate drivers and hazards, including flood, coastal inundation, landslide, maritime extreme weather, and lightning, under baseline and projection periods to support risk-informed adaptation and resilience planning for diverse energy infrastructure. The assessment integrates science-based climate analysis, hazard mapping, and Health, Safety, Security, and Environment (HSSE) risk evaluation. Historical climate data (1983–2011) and future projections (2031–2060) were downscaled to establish atmospheric and marine climate baselines for Southern Sumatra, Western Java, and Central Sulawesi. Probabilistic models were applied to map flood, coastal inundation, landslide, maritime extreme weather, and lightning hazards. Asset exposure from upstream E&P, refinery, and retail and distribution facilities was overlaid with hazard zones, followed by risk scoring using Pertamina probability-impact criteria and Risk Priority Number (RPN). Adaptation options were formulated through the PDCA-based risk management process. The results show distinct physical climate risk characteristics across business units and regions. In Southern Sumatra, upstream E&P assets are primarily exposed to flood, landslide, and lightning hazards, reflecting inland topography and increasing extreme rainfall intensity. Refinery and retail and distribution facilities in Western Java demonstrate elevated risk from coastal inundation and maritime extreme weather due to low elevation and proximity to the northern Java coastline. papers.title: Complementarity of Empirical, Analytical and Numerical Techniques for Assessing the Stability of a Natural Cave System in the Coastal Cliffs of Las Grutas (Río Negro, Argentina)
papers.summary: Coastal caves developed in weak and heterogeneous cliffs constitute complex geomechanical systems in which lithological variability, structural discontinuities, groundwater seepage and marine erosion interact. Their stability assessment is particularly challenging in urbanised coastal and touristic attractive environments, where local failures may affect infrastructure and public safety. This study presents an integrated assessment of a natural cave system in the coastal cliffs of Las Grutas, Río Negro, Argentina. Field observations, structural mapping, geomechanical characterisation and UAV-based three-dimensional reconstruction were combined with empirical classifications, analytical roof-stability methods, and two- and three-dimensional hydro-mechanical numerical modelling. Parameter uncertainty was further explored through probabilistic sensitivity analyses. The results show that the different approaches provide complementary rather than directly interchangeable information. Empirical methods identify sectors with high geomechanical susceptibility, whereas the analytical assessment clarifies the roof-failure mechanisms associated with cavity geometry and stratification. Numerical modelling highlights the stabilising influence of three-dimensional stress redistribution while showing that groundwater flow and discontinuities control the localisation of deformation and the development of potential failure zones. The analyses also indicate that groundwater conditions exert a major influence on the calculated stability margins. Overall, the cliff system remains globally stable under the steady-state hydraulic and monotonic loading conditions considered, although local instability and progressive degradation may develop where basal weakening, seepage and unfavourable discontinuities interact. The study demonstrates the value of critically integrating empirical, analytical and numerical approaches and provides a transferable framework for the assessment and management

papers.summary: ABSTRACT This study unravels the articulation of environmental crises in 13 Indonesian newspaper short stories published between 2023 and 2025 through Greg Garrard’s ecocriticism framework. The study aims to describe and analyze the representation of ecological issues based on the tropes of pollution, wilderness, apocalypse, and animals, in order to deconstruct anthropocentric perspectives in literature. The corpus was selected using purposive sampling based on inclusion criteria regarding the sufficiency of contemporary environmental crisis discourses in national and regional print media. Utilizing a descriptive qualitative approach with note-taking techniques and descriptive-interpretive analysis, 28 textual data units were identified, demonstrating the dominance of the apocalypse category with 10 data units (35.7%) manifesting in floods, landslides, abrasion, and extreme droughts. The pollution category comprises 7 data units (25.0%) representing haze exposure and industrial residues, wilderness accounts for 5 data units (17.9%) related to deforestation and forest exploitation, while animals includes 4 data units (14.3%) regarding habitat fragmentation and threats of species extinction. In addition, 2 data units (7.1%) emerged as additional findings depicting mangrove restoration efforts and indigenous area protection. These findings reinforce the position of newspaper short stories as reflective spaces that potentially foster public ecological awareness, while simultaneously enriching the integration of fiction into Indonesian language pedagogy. papers.title: DS-InSAR combined with dual-attention enhanced CNN-BiGRU for deformation prediction of typical landslides in the Jinsha River Basin
papers.summary: Accurate prediction of step-like abrupt landslide deformation is critical for disaster early warning but remains hindered by the over-smoothing bias of conventional models. This study proposes an end-to-end prediction framework integrating Distributed Scatterer InSAR (DS-InSAR) monitoring data with a dual-attention enhanced CNN-BiGRU network. Two architectures—direct-output and Sequence-to-Sequence (Seq2Seq)—were validated on the Guoba Landslide, a large landslide in the Jinsha River Basin. The dual attention mechanism adaptively isolates critical precursor features, enhancing both precision and interpretability. A global evaluation across all measurement points delineates their domains of applicability. The direct-output DA-CNN-BiGRU acts as a robust spatial filter, achieving a global R2 of 0.92 for ubiquitous continuous creep. Conversely, the Seq2Seq-DA-CNN-BiGRU is specifically optimised to mitigate this over-smoothing bias and capture severe step-like deformations, achieving an R2 of 0.636 at a representative critical point where baselines fail. Across representative kinematic points, it reduces average RMSE and MAE by 24.02% and 30.04%, respectively, compared to standard CNN-BiGRU. This study provides a targeted, interpretable early-warning scheme for complex landslides in high-altitude canyon regions.

papers.title: Flood risk perception and behavioural responses in conditions of repeated floods: evidence from Bagnacavallo (Ravenna, Italy)
Coupled influence of particle shape and basal configuration on rheology of granular media impacting against slit dam
papers.summary: Particle shape and basal boundary conditions play a crucial role in determining mobility, deposition, and impact response of granular flows; yet their coupled influence remains largely unexplored. To this end, we investigate rheology of dry granular media interacting with slit dam within a 3D discrete element setting with varying grain shapes and basal configurations. Besides spherical particles, we consider Platonic solids, viz., dodecahedron, octahedron, and tetrahedron, to explicitly isolate influence of particle morphological features, e.g., sphericity ( ψ ), as these shapes possess identical convexity and aspect ratio while differing primarily in various sphericity measures. Furthermore, we vary basal slip using plane smooth (PS), plane rough (PR), and undulated rough (UR) basal configurations. Comprehensive examination of flow kinematics, kinetics, and grain-scale signatures reveals that decreasing ψ suppresses flow mobility through enhanced particle interlocking and restricted rotation, thereby increasing residual force on barrier. With increasing basal roughness from PS to PR followed by UR, basal slip reduced, accompanied by energy dissipation. Analyses of granular temperature, shear rate, coordination number, force-chain evolution, and fabric anisotropy reveal micromechanical origins of observed macroscopic responses. Additionally, dynamic pressure coefficient ( k d ) scales with Froude number, which varies with ψ for different basal configurations via its control on flow velocity and depth, a relationship developed herein across sphericity measures. Interestingly, k d exhibits maximum value for UR configuration despite exhibiting lowest peak impact force resulting from moderate flow depth and velocity. The micro -to– macro insights further aid in improving impact-force prediction, thereby promoting enhanced design of landslide mitigation structures.

papers.title: Assessing the probability of rainfall-induced landslides along the vulnerable slope-aligned transportation corridor in Darjeeling-Sikkim Himalayas
papers.summary: Shallow debris slides triggered by rainfall are widely distributed along the NH-10 in the Darjeeling–Sikkim Himalayan region, and most of them are reactive in nature. The Himalayan region is vulnerable to reactivated landslides due to extreme rainfall during the monsoon season. The occurrence of landslides largely depends on rainfall patterns. Therefore, the present study focuses on establishing the probability of landslide events P(A|B) with a certain amount of rainfall intensity (0 ≤ I <15, 15 ≤ I < 35, 35 ≤ I < 55, and I ≥ 55 mm/d) and predicting the expected number of landslide events and the number of landslides in different return periods. To achieve these objectives, a Bayes’ probabilistic approach and the Gumbel method have been employed. The pre-requisite data sets, such as rainfall information has been collected from India Meteorological Department (IMD) and tea garden adjacent to the highway, while landslides data have been gathered from Public Works Department (PWD) of National Highway Division-IX, previous research studies daily newspaper and field surveys for the last 15 years (from January, 2011 to December, 2025). During 8 years (2011–2018), the highway witnessed 666 landslides from 278 landslide events were used to calibrate the models. In that period, total 911 rainfall events have been identified from historical rainfall datasets. Whereas, 33 field-identified landslides that occurred between 2019 to 2025 were used to validate the proposed model. The conditional probability of landslide events for a given rainfall intensity and landslide return periods has been estimated using the Gumbel model along NH-10. In addition, similar estimates have been made for four major lithostratigraphic units that span overs the highway. The results indicate significant variations in landslide probability among lithostratigraphic units. papers.title: Slope stability analysis of a plateau lake under strong earthquake impacts: a case study of Lake Sarez, Tajikistan
papers.summary: Strong earthquakes and complex terrain have produced unstable slopes around Sarez Lake, Tajikistan, threatening the Usoi Dam, downstream ecosystems and residents. Using Sentinel-1 images (September 2022–September 2024), we mapped surface deformation with SBAS-InSAR, classified two-dimensional deformation and integrated GNSS–InSAR data to analyze seismic anomalies. We inverted the focal mechanism using the Okada model, identified deformation zones via K-means and applied random forest–SHAP to assess environmental factors’ relative contributions and responses. The results show that horizontal motion dominates regional deformation, while seismic activity significantly induces slope instability. Three-dimensional deformation reveals slow lakeward movement of the Usoi Dam and slopes on both banks. The Mw 6.85 earthquake involved left-lateral strike-slip motion, with nearly E–W compression and N–S extension characterizing regional tectonic stress. Clustering places the Usoi Dam in a stable zone, with vertical subsidence dominating the left-bank slope and westward horizontal motion dominating the right-bank slope. Environmental statistics reveal marked topographic and geological differences among deformation zones. These findings provide quantitative evidence and remote-sensing support for deformation identification, environmental background analysis and safety risk assessment in alpine landslide-dammed lake regions. An integrated ArcGIS Python toolbox for SCS-CN event runoff estimation and flood screening in data-scarce Ethiopian basins
papers.summary: Flood early warning in data-scarce regions is constrained by sparse gauging and limited modelling capacity. We present an integrated ArcGIS Python toolbox automating SCS-CN event runoff estimation, from curve number generation and per-event antecedent moisture classification through to threshold calibration, evaluated in a semi-arid Ethiopian basin. From four quality-controlled stations, 587 rainfall events (2010–2023) were extracted; 98.6% occurred under dry antecedent conditions, corroborated by ERA5-Land soil moisture ( p < 0.001). Evaluation used nineteen documented flood windows from disaster databases and official reports, since discharge records are unavailable. Basin-mean runoff discriminated documented floods with AUC = 0.91 (95% CI 0.83–0.97; Cohen’s d = 2.6), rising to 0.95 for the eleven events triggered within the gauged area. A calibrated 1.25 mm runoff threshold detected thirteen of sixteen floods with approximately 62% fewer false alarms than the regional 30 mm rainfall criterion at equal detection, confirmed out-of-sample by temporal hold-out. Discrimination proved robust to the initial abstraction ratio and ± 10% curve number bias, whereas absolute thresholds were not, making local calibration essential. Limited gauge coverage and a small documented-event sample are acknowledged limitations, quantified via satellite-precipitation comparison and bootstrap intervals. The toolbox provides a transparent, reproducible flood-screening framework for data-scarce semi-arid basins.

papers.title: Integrated Earthquake-Induced Stability Assessment of Lam Chae Earth Dam using Sentinel-1 DInSAR and Field Instrumentation
papers.summary: The Mw 7.7 Myanmar earthquake of 28 March 2025 generated ground shaking across several regions of Thailand, including Nakhon Ratchasima Province, where the Lam Chae Earth Dam is located. Rapid and reliable assessment of dam stability following seismic events is essential for ensuring public safety and supporting reservoir operation. In this context, Sentinel-1 Differential Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (DInSAR) provides spatially continuous deformation measurements over large areas and complements conventional point-based field monitoring instruments. This study presents an integrated assessment of earthquake-induced dam stability using Sentinel-1 DInSAR together with field instrumentation, including inclinometers and piezometers. Sentinel-1 synthetic aperture radar (SAR) images acquired during the pre-seismic, co-seismic, and post-seismic periods were processed to derive line-of-sight (LOS) surface deformation and compared with in-situ monitoring data. The DInSAR analysis revealed a maximum cumulative LOS displacement ranging from approximately - 27 to - 30 mm during the co-seismic period, whereas inclinometer measurements indicated internal deformation ranging from - 1.258 to - 3.980 mm. Piezometer observations confirmed that pore-water pressure remained within the normal operating range throughout the monitoring period. Although DInSAR measurements are subject to uncertainties associated with atmospheric delay, temporal decorrelation, and vegetation-induced coherence loss, the observed deformation patterns were consistent with field measurements, providing complementary evidence for assessing dam behaviour. This study demonstrates the applicability of integrating satellite-based DInSAR with conventional geotechnical instrumentation for post-earthquake dam safety assessment in Thailand, where such integrated applications remain limited. papers.title: Peer Review Report For: Physical and Mechanical Characteristics of Soil as a Controlling Factor in Landslides in Curug Panjang Village, Cihuni Hamlet, Lebak, Banten: Analysis of Distribution, Normality, and Inter-parameter Relationships [version 2; peer review: 1 approved, 2 approved with reservations]
papers.summary: Background Landslide occurrence is strongly influenced by the physical and mechanical properties of subsurface soil; this study evaluates these properties in residual soil from Kampung Cihuni, Lebak Regency, as a controlling factor in landslides. Methods Thirty residual soil samples were collected at a depth of 0–1 m using a grid sampling method. Laboratory testing covered natural water content (w); specific gravity and unit weight, used to derive void ratio (e); the plasticity index (PI) from the Atterberg limits; and Unconsolidated Undrained (UU) triaxial testing for cohesion (c) and internal friction angle (φ). The distribution of each parameter was evaluated using histograms, Q-Q plots, and the Shapiro-Wilk normality test, while inter-parameter relationships were analysed using linear regression (R 2 ) and Spearman correlation (ρ). Results The Shapiro-Wilk test showed that cohesion (c) and void ratio (e) are normally distributed, whereas water content (w), PI, and friction angle (φ) are not. PI values for the plastic samples (n = 26) ranged from 13.8% to 86.7%, and φ ranged from 5.48° to 20.5°; the relationship between the two was weakly positive (R 2 = 0.151, p = 0.050; Spearman ρ = 0.244, p = 0.229). Cohesion ranged from 4.41–52.47 kPa but showed a very weak, non-significant relationship with water content (R 2 = 0.028, p = 0.376), as did void ratio with φ (R 2 = 0.089, p = 0.110). Conclusions Relationships among the physical and mechanical parameters were weak and mostly non-significant, so the reduction in soil shear strength cannot be explained by any single parameter alone. Because the UU triaxial test represents total-stress conditions, it cannot directly explain rainfall infiltration and pore-water pressure change as a landslide trigger, though it offers an initial picture of the residual soil’s engineering characteristics as a controlling factor in the area’s landslide susceptibility.

papers.title: A dynamic warning system for single-gully debris flows in Beijing mountain areas: model construction and performance verification
papers.summary: Debris flows in Beijing's mountainous areas feature sudden occurrence and high destructiveness, posing severe threats to residents' lives and property. Conventional early warning models based only on regional rainfall thresholds or static susceptibility suffer from low spatial resolution, high false alarm rates, and poor timeliness. This study develops a mechanism-inspired statistical dynamic early warning model for single-gully debris flows using multi-dimensional controlling factors and historical disaster data (2016–2022). The model establishes a composite geological index from four core indicators and a rainfall index using maximum hourly rainfall intensity and event-based cumulative rainfall. A power-law nonlinear coupling relationship is optimized via grid search, and a four-level graded warning system is constructed. Validated by three extreme rainfall events (2023–2025), the model achieves a Probability of Detection exceeding 97%, a false alarm rate below 5%, a critical success index above 0.80, and an average warning lead time of 1.2–1.5 hours. It has been implemented in the Beijing Geological Hazard Monitoring and Early Warning System for real-time operation. This work enables a shift from regional to refined single-gully warning, providing technical support for disaster mitigation and a transferable framework for similar urban mountainous regions worldwide.

papers.title: Study on three-dimensional deformation monitoring of railway slopes via synergistic integration of Beidou and InSAR
papers.summary: Abstract Remote-sensing-based slope stability monitoring is vital for railway safety. This study is grounded in the demands for high timeliness and multi-element monitoring of three-dimensional deformation of modern railway slopes. Aiming at the issue that existing technologies struggle to balance spatial and temporal resolution in the process of fusing and resolving three-dimensional deformation using the BeiDou Navigation Satellite System (BDS) and Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR), a point-surface hierarchical fusion strategy is proposed. After constructing a unified fused observation equation, spatial regularization constraints and local joint adjustment are introduced to balance spatiotemporal resolution from two levels. This ensures the consistency and reliability of 3D accuracy under the hierarchical strategy, while achieves constrained representation of the large-scale deformation trend and high-precision temporal evolution of the 3D deformation field. Building on the hierarchical fusion results, this paper proposes a 3D deformation risk classification method for railway slopes, enabling refined slope monitoring and early disaster warning with a feasible technical scheme. The effectiveness of the method is validated on typical slopes along the Shijiazhuang-Taiyuan Railway. The results indicated that (1) the average 3D deformation accuracy obtained by the point–surface hierarchical fusion strategy is superior to 10 mm, ensuring both accuracy balance and reliability under the hierarchical strategy while taking into account both spatial and temporal resolutions. (2) The proposed three-dimensional deformation risk classification method for slopes preliminarily verifies the feasibility of the hierarchical fusion strategy for 3D deformation monitoring of railway slopes considering both spatial and temporal resolutions.

papers.title: Analysis of stability influencing factors and failure mechanism of anti-dip rock slope under strong earthquake
papers.summary: Anti-dip rock slope is a common layered rock slope, and the failure mechanism of it under strong earthquake is not well studied. In order to analyze the stability and failure mode of anti-dip rock slope under strong earthquake, this paper investigates 60 typical failure cases of anti-dip rock slope, analyzes the effect of factors on slope stability, and summarizes the failure mode. Taking the Hongshiyan slope as an example, the dynamic response law of the slope under earthquake action was summarized, and the failure mechanism of the slope was studied. Finally, the sensitivity of each influencing factor was analyzed through orthogonal experiments. The results show that the failure mode of the anti-dip rock slope with hard rocks upper and soft rocks lower is the shear slip of the soft rock at the bottom and the tensile cracking and topplingfailure of the hard rock at the top. The influencing factors ranked in descending order of sensitivity are as follows: slope angle, seismic wave frequency, inclination, seismic wave amplitude, slope shape coefficient, and slope height. It is of great significance to study the failure mode of anti-dip rock slope under strong earthquake and evaluate its stability for slope disaster prevention and control in infrastructure engineering.

papers.title: Geologically constrained dynamic evolution and early warning of urban resource-environment carrying capacity: a case study of Jinan, China
papers.summary: Urban resource environment carrying capacity (RECC) is increasingly challenged by nonlinear interactions among socioeconomic development, resource depletion, and geological environmental degradation. However, existing assessments often neglect the cumulative feedback effects of groundwater depletion and geological responses. This study develops a city-scale system dynamics (SD) model integrating six subsystems (population–economy, land, water resources, ecology, environment, and geological environment) to simulate RECC evolution in Jinan, China, during 2021–2031. A groundwater–geological feedback module is incorporated to explicitly represent the interactions among groundwater abstraction, groundwater depletion, land subsidence, and development constraints. A scenario-based early-warning framework is further developed to identify nonlinear degradation trajectories under alternative scenarios. Model validation indicates satisfactory performance, with R² and NSE values ranging from 0.87 to 0.97. Results reveal a transition from development-driven expansion to resource- and geo-environmental constraint regulation. Under the business-as-usual scenario, available water resources decline by 40%, the groundwater recovery index reaches − 0.35, land subsidence increases by 25%, and RECC declines by 28% by 2031. Water and geo-environmental constraints jointly contribute 71% of total RECC limitations, and a critical groundwater stress threshold is identified at approximately 1.15 (groundwater recovery index = − 0.15), beyond which degradation accelerates. Compared with business-as-usual, the resource-optimization scenario increases available water resources by 56%, reduces water pollution by 64% and land subsidence by 31%, delays high-level warnings by 2–3 years, and maintains 92% of per-capita GDP. These findings highlight the importance of groundwater–geological feedbacks for dynamic RECC assessment and sustainable urban planning.

papers.title: Reply on RC2
papers.summary: Abstract. La Réunion is one of the French territories most exposed to natural risks. The island is exposed to seven major natural hazards: cyclones, floods, swells and tsunamis, landslides, earthquakes, wildfires, and volcanic eruptions. Numerous natural disasters have occurred on the island, as well as less significant natural events. This study presents a historical review of the direct impacts of natural events documented in departmental and national archives since human settlement on the island. Thus, in total 2,823 sources, referencing 1,266 events from 1655 to 2025 have been processed. The source's reliability is analyzed using a decision tree method. Based on the impacts, significance scores for each referenced event is established. An analysis of the evolution of impacts and mortality over time is conducted. A detailed geodatabase (HistoRiskRun) is created to capitalize information about natural hazards in La Réunion since its colonization. This database enhances documentation and understanding of past events and the evolution of risk management over time. This work provides elements to discuss the temporal evolution of impacts and mortalities associated with natural hazards and to relate these dynamics to the island’s geo-socio-historical context.

papers.title: geofm-landslide-benchmark: cross-model evaluation protocol and derived datasets for geospatial foundation models in landslide susceptibility
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: Reproducibility package for 'What survives an audit: evaluating geospatial foundation models for landslide susceptibility against a geomorphometric baseline' (in preparation for Earth Science Informatics). The code (tag v1.4.0) implements the cross-model benchmark of TerraMind and Prithvi-EO-2.0 against a 17-layer geomorphometric baseline under spatial-block cross-validation, with the random-initialization ablation, point-probe controls (context-matched manual baselines, spectral scar probe, constrained-negative sensitivity), the control arms (ground motion, movement typology, geology, climate), and the audit re-analyses (positional floor on the benchmark folds for every pipeline, range of spatial dependence against the block size, variance of the negative draw and of the block-grid placement, readers tuned by nested spatial cross-validation), together with the table and figure generators and the per-fold result files (JSON) behind every reported number. The deposit adds the derived datasets: 17-layer geomorphometric feature stacks (npz) for five Chilean basins, annual 2023 Sentinel-2 L2A composites (GeoTIFF) built per MGRS tile for Huasco, Maipo and Maule, the sampled benchmark points with spatial-block ids (CSV), the Prithvi input patches of those points (uint16 memmaps) and the Maule fold indices. data/ZENODO_DEPOSIT.md documents every file. The transformer-block sweep, low-rank adaptation, the pre-/post-event test and the Prithvi susceptibility surfaces predate the Prithvi input-offset correction; their result files are kept in the code for traceability but are not reported.

papers.title: LD-DETR: A Multi-Scale Landslide Detection and Segmentation Network for Complex Geological Environments
papers.summary: Landslides are among the most destructive natural hazards. High-resolution remote sensing imagery provides an effective means for landslide detection and mapping, supporting geological hazard assessment and early warning. However, existing methods still face challenges in complex mountainous scenes with heterogeneous land cover and geological conditions. These challenges include irregular segmentation boundaries caused by diverse landslide shapes, small-scale detection difficulties due to background interference, and foreground–background class imbalance that hinders effective model optimization. To address these issues, we propose LD-DETR, a network for landslide detection and segmentation. An Atrous Spatial Pyramid Pooling (ASPP) module is integrated into the segmentation head to improve multi-scale feature representation, enabling better segmentation of landslides with varying spatial sizes. To alleviate class imbalance caused by the dominance of non-landslide pixels, a weighted Tversky Loss is introduced to improve the learning of hard samples. Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is further combined with orientation-aware data augmentation to enable parameter-efficient adaptation, reducing the proportion of trainable parameters of LD-DETR to 41.07% while keeping the pre-trained backbone parameters frozen. Experiments on the Bijie and Luding Landslide Dataset (BLLD) demonstrate that LD-DETR is competitive with the baseline model and several YOLO-based approaches. The proposed method achieves an F1-score of 95.18% and a Recall of 95%, while the segmentation task reaches an mAP of 59.28%, slightly higher than the RF-DETR baseline. Furthermore, a limited-sample adaptation experiment on the Jiuzhai landslide dataset demonstrates the transferability of the proposed method across different geographic regions. These results indicate that the proposed framework provides competitive landslide detection and segmentation performance and offers an approach for fine-grained landslide

papers.title: A pseudo-three-dimensional work-balance correction for sidewall friction effects in centrifuge slope models
papers.summary: Abstract Centrifuge model tests are widely used to investigate slope stability; however, frictional interactions between the sliding mass and rigid container sidewalls introduce boundary effects that compromise similitude with ideal plane-strain prototypes. These effects can lead to an apparent increase in the stability of finite-width models relative to the corresponding plane-strain reference. In this paper, a pseudo-three-dimensional work-balance correction based on a classical plane-strain upper-bound mechanism is developed by introducing an additional out-of-plane sidewall-friction work-rate term evaluated from an assumed lateral normal-stress distribution into the global work rate balance. A random-search optimisation technique is employed to identify the critical failure surface geometry and the corresponding stability factor. The proposed formulation is checked against the classical plane-strain upper-bound solution and further compared with published centrifuge test data. Across the reported configurations, the calculated and measured critical acceleration scale factors show the same decreasing trends with increasing model height and slope inclination, although substantial differences remain for individual cases. A parametric study reveals that sidewall friction significantly increases the apparent stability factor at low width-to-height ratios, but this discrepancy diminishes rapidly as the ratio increases. For the representative cases examined at β = 60°, the sidewall friction angle and width-to-height ratio exert larger influences on the sidewall-induced relative deviation than the soil internal friction angle, while the influence of the soil internal friction angle is retained explicitly in the broader reference charts and tables. Reference charts and tables are further developed to quantify the width-dependent deviation for selected parameter combinations and relative-deviation thresholds. These resources provide preliminary, assumption-dependent refer

papers.title: Integrating earth observation and machine learning for forest fire risk assessment in Rasuwa district, Nepal
papers.summary: The complex terrain and increasing forest fire incidents in recent years make high-mountain environments vulnerable to forest fires, posing a threat to ecological and economic well-being. However, research related to forest fires remains limited in the mountain region. The study aimed to assess the forest fire risk by integrating eleven predictive layers (biophysical, topographical, climatic, and anthropogenic factors) and a Random Forest (RF) model in Rasuwa, a mountainous district of Nepal. However, the precipitation factor was excluded due to multicollinearity concerns. The model was validated using Area Under the Curve (AUC) and True Skill Statistics (TSS). With an AUC of 0.9 and TSS of 0.67, the model shows strong predictive performance and high reliability of the generated fire risk map. The most significant factors in the model’s ability to predict the forest fire risk were elevation, temperature, Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), and proximity to settlements. The study shows that 29.66% of Rasuwa district’s forest is at fire risk, with the highest risk in Kalika Rural Municipality (53.7%). In the study area, approximately 30% of fire incidents occurred at elevations above 3000 m. The results can assist the concerned stakeholders and authorities in developing effective forest management plans by prioritizing identified high-risk areas for early warning systems and fuel management.

papers.title: Uso de técnicas edafológicas en el estudio de condiciones ambientales antiguas y de cultivos indígenas en el Ecoparque Golondrinas, Andes Colombianos
papers.summary: The Golondrinas archaeological site is in the Colombian inter-Andean Aburrá Valley hillslopes (2,000 m a.s.l). The initial archaeological assessment presented here included field observations, archaeological survey, soil chemistry, palynology, and micromorphological analyses in five locations, to identify a representative site. The complete pedostratigraphic sequence was analyzed to characterize depositional and post-depositional processes and to evaluate the effects of pedoturbation, pedogenesis, and anthropogenic features in relation to paleohydrological information. The archaeological record was assessed through a soil profile representative of the Golondrinas site (3,800 m2) described at microscale. The results provide a basis for testing hypotheses and proposing interpretations about past ecological conditions and historical land use dynamics at the study site. The findings and soil analyses suggest a history of land use that may have been associated with relatively high biological activity and high organic carbon content under hydromorphic conditions, as well as with alternating phases of agricultural activity and natural forest cover in the past. The study also identifies the presence of significant surface water flows and episodes of landslide activity associated with the site's geomorphological setting, which may have influenced both historical and contemporary land-use patterns.
