THEORETICAL AND METHODOLOGICAL FOUNDATIONS OF MONITORING HAZARDOUS GEOLOGICAL PROCESSES
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: This article discusses the theoretical and methodological foundations of monitoring hazardous geological processes. Natural and anthropogenic factors influencing the formation and development of landslides, subsidence, displacement, deformation and other geological processes are analyzed. Modern approaches to monitoring hazardous geological processes are considered, including geodetic observations, remote sensing technologies, synthetic aperture radar interferometry, multispectral optical imagery and geographic information systems. The integration of data from different sources provides opportunities to identify hazardous areas, assess the spatial and temporal development of geological processes and improve the reliability of monitoring results.

papers.title: Rainfall Prediction Using a Hybrid CNN-LSTM Method to Support Hydrometeorological Disaster Mitigation in Bima Regency
papers.summary: Rainfall is one of the key meteorological parameters that significantly influences the occurrence of hydrometeorological disasters, such as floods and landslides, particularly in Bima Regency, which has a high level of vulnerability due to climate variability. Accurate rainfall prediction is essential for supporting decision-making in disaster mitigation and water resource management. This study aims to develop a rainfall prediction model using a Hybrid Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)–Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) approach that effectively captures both the spatial and temporal characteristics of meteorological data. The dataset consists of historical rainfall records along with supporting meteorological variables collected from observation stations over a specified period. The research methodology includes data preprocessing, normalization using the Min-Max Scaling method, time series data construction, development of the Hybrid CNN–LSTM model, model training and testing, and performance evaluation using Mean Absolute Error (MAE), Root Mean Square Error (RMSE), and Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) metrics. The results indicate that the proposed Hybrid CNN–LSTM model provides accurate rainfall predictions by effectively extracting local features through CNN layers and capturing long-term temporal dependencies through LSTM layers. Furthermore, the proposed model demonstrates more stable performance in predicting rainfall fluctuations compared with conventional approaches, making it a promising solution for supporting early warning systems and decision-making in hydrometeorological disaster mitigation in Bima Regency. Therefore, the application of the Hybrid CNN–LSTM method offers an effective artificial intelligence-based approach to improving rainfall prediction accuracy.

papers.title: Quantifying volumetric erosion from symbolic expression of landslide morphology
papers.summary: Landslide volumetric erosion is fundamental to regional sediment budgets and downstream hazard assessment, yet accurately constraining material mobilization remains a primary bottleneck in Earth-system research. Legacy area–volume relations introduce substantial uncertainty when applied across heterogeneous landslide populations. Here, we examine whether the erosional and accumulation (i.e., runout) domains provide information beyond source area alone for volumetric erosion. Using neural-guided symbolic regression, we identify an expression that preserves source area as the first-order control on erosional volume while introducing a dimensionless descriptor of the accumulation counterpart, as a geometric correction. For the 2016 Kaikōura earthquake inventory, the framework estimates a cumulative eroded volume of 54.9 Mm3, compared with the measured 56.5 Mm3. The formulation was additionally applied without recalibration to the independent 2018 Hokkaidō inventory and subsequently used for blind inference on 32 landslides from the 2013 Lushan earthquake, yielding a cumulative estimate of 1.95 Mm3 of volumetric erosion. Because independent volume observations are unavailable for Lushan, this application is treated as inference rather than external validation. Polygon-generalization experiments further indicate that our new formulation remains stable across different mapping resolutions. These results show that scale-normalized planform geometry can provide complementary information to source area when constraining landslide erosion. The proposed framework is therefore intended as an empirical extension to, rather than a replacement for, established area–volume scaling.

papers.title: Correlating InSAR-derived ground movement rates with landslide activity class and causal factors: a case study from Cyprus
papers.summary: Abstract This study investigates the statistical correlation between ground movement rates in landslide areas, as derived by Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR) results, with geological, geomorphological, environmental and geotechnical causal factors in southwestern Cyprus. The analysis examines ground velocities derived using Multi-Temporal Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (MT-InSAR) for both active and inactive landslides that are recorded in an existing inventory, using ascending and descending orbit datasets. The results show that the largest Line-of-Sight (LOS) velocities are observed in landslides characterized as active, followed by dormant and relict landslides. The largest displacement rates correspond mostly to outcrops of fine-grained clastic rocks, such as marls, radiolarian mudstones and mélange, due to their weak shear strength. An analysis based on Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) identified rainfall as the primary factor influencing the increase in LOS velocity. The Plasticity Index (PI) generally exhibits a positive correlation with the velocity, while the Geological Strength Index (GSI) demonstrates a weak negative correlation. The findings suggest that, while geological and geotechnical characteristics are crucial in the emergence of landslide phenomena, the rate of the ground movement, once initiated, is predominantly influenced by the precipitation height.

papers.title: Adaptive Timing of Landslide Susceptibility Map Updates Using Persistent Deformation Changes
papers.summary: Interferometric synthetic aperture radar (InSAR) provides spatially extensive deformation measurements that support dynamic landslide susceptibility assessment. However, determining when landslide susceptibility maps require updating remains insufficiently studied. Here, we introduce the persistent deformation-change area ratio (PDAR), the percentage of monitored slope-unit area exhibiting persistent velocity changes relative to each unit’s accepted reference. Three-observation confirmation and reference resetting allow update intervals to respond to both increasing and decreasing deformation. A common asymmetric matrix combines the current susceptibility class with the relative velocity change, allowing at most two upward steps or one downward step. We compared PDAR with no updating and fixed one-, three-, six- and twelve-month schedules across 6956 slope units in Yunyang, Kaizhou and Wushan. Baseline construction used 2013–2016, parameter calibration used 2017–2018, and evaluation covered 2019–2022. PDAR achieved the highest area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC-AUC; 0.7913 versus 0.6848 without updating), highest high/very high event capture (63.99%) and lowest false-positive rate (FPR; 13.67%). Relative to monthly updating, AUC increased by 0.1162 and FPR decreased by 12.92 percentage points. PDAR also exceeded the strongest fixed schedule, six-month updating, by 0.0688 in AUC. The fixed-window comparison showed that more frequent updating was not always beneficial. PDAR provides a state-dependent basis for selecting update windows rather than updating whenever newer observations become available.

papers.title: PENGEMBANGAN MEDIA PEMBELAJARAN DIGITAL FLIPBOOK UNTUK MENUMBUHKAN KESADARAN MITIGASI BENCANA TANAH LONGSOR PADA ANAK USIA DINI DI TK NEGERI PEMBINA SITIUNG
papers.summary: The importance of disaster education for early childhood cannot be overlooked, particularly in disaster-prone areas such as Dharmasraya Regency, West Sumatra. Unfortunately, learning activities in kindergartens often face a common challenge, namely the limited availability of child-friendly and interactive learning media. In response to this issue, this study was designed to develop the digital flipbook “Ayo Siaga Longsor” and to examine its validity, practicality, and effectiveness in fostering landslide mitigation awareness among students at TK Negeri Pembina Sitiung. A Research and Development (R&D) method based on the ADDIE framework (Analysis, Design, Development, Implementation, and Evaluation) was employed as the research framework. The study involved material, media, and language validators, classroom teachers, and Group B students of TK Negeri Pembina Sitiung as research subjects. Data were collected through validation instruments, teacher response questionnaires, and pre-test and post-test assessments, and were subsequently analyzed using a quantitative descriptive approach. The results confirmed that the digital flipbook achieved a validity score of 88.33%, categorized as very valid, while its practicality based on the teacher’s response reached 90%, categorized as very practical. Its effectiveness was demonstrated by a substantial increase in the children’s understanding, with the mean pre-test score increasing from 39.5% to 85.25% in the post-test, resulting in an N-Gain index of 0.76, which falls into the high category. In conclusion, the digital flipbook “Ayo Siaga Longsor” was proven to be valid, practical, and effective as an alternative learning medium for fostering disaster mitigation awareness among young children from an early age.

papers.title: Effect of Rainfall Infiltration on the Hydromechanical Behavior of Slopes under Unsaturated Conditions
papers.summary: Nowadays, slopes forming transportation infrastructure are highly sensitive to hydraulic conditions such as rainfall, triggering negative impacts on ecosystems and road infrastructure. In this regard, this research analyzes the hydromechanical influence of a frequent rainfall intensity in northern Peru of 10 mm/h on the stability of slopes (T1, T2, and T3) under unsaturated conditions. For this purpose, simulations were performed using Plaxis 2D software, considering three slope geometries based on regulatory criteria for clayey gravel soils with fines content and groundwater table conditions. The input parameters for the soil were based on the Hardening Soil model, while the Van Genuchten model was used for flow analysis. The obtained results indicate that, within the analyzed section measured from the upper surface downward, maximum saturation reached a depth equivalent to 33% of the slope height for model T1, 11.8% for model T2, and 6.4% for model T3. In addition, the effective surface suction produced reductions lower than 3 kN/m² after 24 hours of continuous rainfall. Finally, the factor of safety was affected under the same scenario, decreasing by up to 59.11% for model T1, 49.2% for model T2, and 42.80% for model T3. It should be noted that the most significant transition toward instability occurred after 10 hours.

papers.title: Analysis of Landslide Susceptibility Toward the Presence of Accommodation Areas (Glamping and Villas) in Kejajar District, Wonosobo Regency, 2025
papers.summary: This study aims to analyze and map the level of landslide susceptibility in accommodation areas in Kejajar District, Wonosobo Regency, using a Geographic Information System (GIS) approach. Scoring, weighting, and overlay methods were applied to integrate rainfall, slope gradient, soil type, geology, and land-use parameters. The results indicate that Kejajar District is divided into three landslide susceptibility classes: high susceptibility covering 4,936 ha (76%), moderate susceptibility covering 1,515 ha (23%), and low susceptibility covering 37 ha (<1%). Spatial analysis of accommodation areas indicates that most villas and glamping facilities are located in moderate-to-high susceptibility zones, particularly in areas with steep slopes, high rainfall, and easily weathered soil materials. These findings emphasize the importance of using landslide susceptibility maps as a basis for spatial planning and disaster mitigation guidance in the development of highland tourism areas.

papers.title: How past natural disturbances and human land use dynamics shape the current structure and composition of moist Afromontane forests
papers.summary: Historical knowledge of the landscape is essential to understand the current ecosystem. We studied how common natural disturbances and land use changes are, and how these histories affect current forest structure and tree species composition. We used data from 44 key informant interviews and inventories from 125 forest sites. Regarding natural disturbances, we found that they are rather infrequent, even if there are reports from many places of occasional wildfires, storms causing windfalls, landslides and various dieback of trees. Shade coffee management at various intensities is common throughout the forests at elevations where coffee can be grown. Part of the area has been subjected to logging. There is evidence of rather widespread abandonment in the late 19th century, but also more recent abandonments. Hence, some areas that now are forested have previously been settlements and open farmland areas. These natural disturbances and land uses histories are highly diverse, resulting in heterogeneous influence on the current forest structure and tree species composition. For example sites, with current coffee management have less lianas and somewhat different trees than sites regenerated after large scale disturbances. We conclude that current structure and composition of forests are the outcomes of diverse current and historical human land use management practices. Given that large scale natural disturbances are rather infrequent, the base-line landscape was likely dominated by undisturbed forests. Thus, conservation strategies should explicitly target undisturbed stands alongside the sustainable utilization of resources.

papers.title: Alertas tempranas de bajo costo para carreteras rurales centroamericanas: revisión sistemática
papers.summary: Flash floods and debris flows can sever rural roads within minutes, while sparse gauges, uneven telecommunications and limited maintenance constrain conventional warning systems. This review synthesized low-cost early warning technologies and derived requirements transferable to Central American corridors. A systematic search covered publications from 2008-2025 and was supplemented by backward and forward citation tracking. Eligible records had to provide real-time monitoring or decision functions, a reproducible architecture, and evidence applicable to flash floods, lahars, debris flows or rapid landslides. The 21 included studies were appraised across eight technical and operational domains. Fourteen addressed flooding and seven rapid slope processes; nine were rated high quality, ten moderate and two low. Rain gauges, water-level sensors, geophones, infrasound, GSM/SMS, LoRa, solar power and local threshold rules predominate. Only one study was explicitly Central American and three directly supported road decisions. Field evidence favors redundancy, edge processing, remote diagnostics and physical road actuation over algorithmic complexity. Life-cycle cost, multi-year availability, drift, false alarms and user response remain poorly reported. A tiered architecture is proposed, combining regional surveillance, local nodes, redundant communications, and pre-closure, closure and reopening protocols.

papers.title: Construction of Ecological Security Patterns and Priority Identification for Restoration in High-Risk Geological Disaster Areas Coupled with InSAR Technology and Neural Network Models
papers.source: International Journal of Image and Graphics
papers.summary: Geological disasters threaten ecological stability, yet restoration planning in high-risk areas remains difficult because deformation, environmental conditions, and hazard drivers vary across space and time. We developed a multimodal dataset, HGR-InSAR-2022, covering 12[Formula: see text]640[Formula: see text]km 2 and comprising 312 Sentinel-1 scenes, 1486 Sentinel-2 images, a 30-m digital elevation model, rainfall and geological layers, and 1276 documented landslide locations collected from 2018 to 2022. The dataset provides comprehensive spatial and temporal observations for characterizing terrain instability, ecological degradation, and heterogeneous environmental responses across disaster-prone landscapes. Based on this dataset, we propose AGRNet, an adaptive geospatial restoration network that integrates a constraint-aware restoration optimizer, an agent-based risk mapping unit, and an uncertainty-driven InSAR fusion module. The network combines InSAR-derived deformation, multispectral ecological indicators, topographic variables, and hazard factors to generate ecological security patterns and restoration-priority maps while quantifying prediction uncertainty. This multimodal integration enables the model to capture complex interactions between surface deformation, ecological conditions, and geological hazard processes at different spatial scales. On an independent 20% test set, AGRNet achieved an [Formula: see text]1-score of 0.91 and an intersection-over-union of 0.84 for ecological security classification, outperforming random forest and conventional convolutional neural network baselines by 8.7 and 5.1 percentage points, respectively. Its restoration-priority map achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.94, while uncertainty modeling reduced deformation prediction RMSE by 16.3%. These results demonstrate that the proposed framework provides accurate, uncertainty-aware support for ecological restoration and geological-disaster

papers.title: The Effect of Collaborative Leadership and Early Warning System on Community Preparedness Response through Community Participation in Madiun Regency
papers.summary: Disaster risks in Madiun Regency, particularly floods, landslides, and tornadoes, underscore the need for preparedness strategies that integrate early warning systems, stakeholder coordination, and community involvement. This study examined the effects of collaborative leadership and early warning systems on community preparedness response, including indirect effects through community participation. A quantitative explanatory design involved 400 respondents from purposively selected areas. Data were collected using a five-point Likert-scale questionnaire and analyzed through partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) using SmartPLS 4. The structural model identified significant paths from collaborative leadership and early warning systems to both preparedness response and community participation. Community participation was positively and significantly associated with preparedness response and partially mediated the relationship between each predictor and preparedness response. These findings identify community participation as an intermediary linking collaborative leadership and early warning systems to preparedness. The study concludes that disaster preparedness efforts should integrate collaborative governance, warning systems, and community participation. The findings provide evidence to inform the strengthening of participatory disaster management policies in Madiun Regency.

papers.title: The deforming and failing Wangzang reservoir bank landslide in the upper–middle reaches of the Bailong River, China
Problems, causes and impacts of landslides along the Beni–Jomsom–Korala Road in the Kaligandaki Corridor, Nepal
papers.source: Universal Technical Journal of Lumbini International Academy of Science and Technology
papers.summary: The Beni–Jomsom–Korala road, part of the Kaligandaki Corridor linking Myagdi and Mustang districts with the northern border of Nepal, is repeatedly blocked by landslides, particularly during the monsoon. This study assessed the major landslide problems along the road, their causes and effects, and the mitigation measures preferred by stakeholders. A mixed-methods design was used, combining field observation of four active landslides (Baisari, Sirubari, Guithe Bhir and Suke Bagar), engineering geological maps of the Khamvitta and Tatopani slides, focus group discussions, in-depth interviews and a five-point Likert questionnaire answered by 120 engineers, contractors, officials and local stakeholders. Items were ranked with the Relative Importance Index (RII); internal consistency was checked with Cronbach’s alpha (0.767–0.921 across the four scales) and relations between constructs with Pearson correlation. River cutting and toe erosion by the Kaligandaki River (RII = 0.80) and cutting of the hillside to carve the road (0.78) were the most important of 19 problems, followed by inadequate drainage, poor lithology and weak geology (0.76 each). The leading causes were steep and unstable slopes (0.82), removal of the slope toe by road widening (0.82), communities living on unstable slopes (0.82), insufficient government funding (0.82) and fractured, weathered rock (0.80). The most important effects were water accumulation on the road causing erosion (0.84), increased casualties when rescue is delayed (0.83), delayed mitigation projects (0.83) and disruption of trade and tourism (0.82). Ratings of causes and effects were very strongly correlated (r = 0.863, p < 0.001). Field evidence confirmed fractured rock, shallow groundwater, river undercutting and blasting damage as the dominant mechanisms. Respondents ranked slope stabilization with retaining and breast walls (0.78), rock anchoring and netting, and roadside bioengineering (0.76 each) as the most important measures.

papers.title: Assessment of Flood Impacts, Losses and Adaptation Practices in Bhajani Municipality, Kailali District, Nepal
papers.source: Universal Technical Journal of Lumbini International Academy of Science and Technology
papers.summary: Floods are the most frequent and damaging hydro-meteorological hazard in the Terai region of Nepal, yet municipal-scale evidence that links hazard mapping, community perception, historical losses and local adaptation remains scarce. This study assesses flood impacts, losses, and adaptation practices in Bhajani Municipality, Kailali District, Sudurpashchim Province, a low-lying municipality with nine wards (176.25 km²) and crossed by the Mohana, Kandra, Kanda (Kadha), and Patharaiya rivers. A mixed-methods design combined a questionnaire survey of 156 respondents (Slovin’s formula, e = 8%), focus group discussions, in-depth interviews, field observation and desk review of the Local Disaster and Climate Resilience Plan (LDCRP). The Relative Importance Index (RII) was used to rank 16 flood-related problems, their causes and effects, and 12 adaptation measures rated on a five-point Likert scale; 64 Chi-square tests of independence examined whether perceptions differ by gender, age, occupation and education, and a GIS-based Weighted Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis (WMCDA) using distance from rivers (30%), Topographic Wetness Index (25%), slope (25%) and Height Above Nearest Drainage (20%) produced a flood hazard map. Wards 3, 5, 7 and 8 were classified as very high flood-risk areas, wards 6 and 9 as high, wards 1 and 2 as moderate and ward 4 as low–moderate; 85 settlements and hamlets are potentially exposed. Sixteen flood events recorded in municipal and community records affected 5,140 households, displaced 598 households, destroyed 188 houses, damaged about 1,695 bighas of cultivable land, caused an estimated loss of NPR 702.4 million and claimed 10 lives. Agriculture damage (RII = 0.863) and livestock damage (0.846) ranked as the most important problems. Non-compliance with flood-resistant building standards (0.914), waterlogging from slow runoff (0.891), insufficient investment in early warning systems (0.854) and weak institutional capacity (0.854) were the leadin

papers.title: Feature-engineered physics-conditioned DNN with validation-selected ridge residual correction for pore water pressure prediction in clays
papers.summary: Introduction Accurately predicting pore water pressure is important for evaluating effective stress, deformation, and stability in clayey soils. Methods This study develops an interpretable feature-engineered physics-conditioned DNN with validation-selected ridge residual correction using 42 complete curves from kaolin clay and Mercia Mudstone clay. Complete curves were divided into training, validation, and testing subsets. Three configurations were compared: a Physics-Conditioned DNN (PC-DNN), a feature-engineered PC-DNN (FE-PC-DNN), and the FE-PC-DNN with a candidate residual stage. Physical knowledge was used to select variables, construct hydro-mechanical interaction features, define a reference response, and bound the correction; governing equations were not enforced in the loss function. Results Validation assigned zero weight to the neural residual candidate and full weight to ridge regression. Accordingly, the reported residual correction was ridge-based, clipped to ±0.419394 kPa, and combined with a validation-bias offset of −0.099064 kPa. The ridge-corrected FE-PC-DNN achieved a test MSE of 1.58 kPa 2 , RMSE of 1.26 kPa, MAE of 0.82 kPa, and sMAPE of 8.75%. Global SHAP analysis identified soil type, axial strain, and confining pressure as the main features. A unified kernel-weighted B-spline equation, calibrated on 36 development curves and evaluated once on six locked test curves, achieved R 2 = 0.982, RMSE = 0.894 kPa, MAE = 0.716 kPa, and sMAPE = 6.03%. Discussion These results demonstrate strong internal performance within the tested two-soil domain; external validation is still required before field use.

papers.title: A Comprehensive County-Scale Dataset for Geohazard Risk Assessment of House Construction via Cutting Slope (HCCS)
papers.summary: House construction via cutting slope (HCCS) is an increasingly important driver of geohazards in the granite weathering regions of southeastern China. In these areas, frequent intense rainfall and the rapid growth of self-built rural housing together contribute to recurring landslides at HCCS sites. However, relevant geo-environmental data are often dispersed across survey reports in non-standardized formats, hindering their integration and reuse in fine-scale spatial analyses. We describe a county-wide geospatial dataset for Yanling County, Hunan Province, China, that links slope units, geohazard inventories, and HCCS sites within a unified spatial framework. The dataset includes 3478 slope units, 213 documented geohazard sites (landslides, debris flows, collapses, and ground subsidence), and 12,420 HCCS sites, as well as supporting layers including a digital elevation model, geological structures, river networks, and administrative boundaries. The data were generated from a 1:10,000 geohazard survey using a standardized workflow covering field investigation, database development, and multi-level review, and were further harmonized through unified coordinate and attribute systems. This dataset provides a rare fine-scale representation of the spatial coupling between anthropogenic slope modification for housing and rainfall-induced landslides at the individual-building scale. It offers a reusable data foundation for landslide susceptibility mapping, risk evaluation of HCCS development, and studies of coupled hazard processes in comparable granite mountainous environments.

papers.title: Comparative Machine Learning Approaches to Landslide Susceptibility in Southeastern Türkiye
papers.summary: Landslides are among the most destructive natural hazards in mountainous regions, causing severe economic losses and infrastructure damage. Reliable susceptibility mapping is essential for hazard mitigation and sustainable land-use planning, particularly in tectonically active areas such as southeastern Türkiye. This study aims to compare the predictive performance and spatial consistency of six widely used machine learning algorithms—Support Vector Machine (SVM), Logistic Regression (LR), Random Forest (RF), Artificial Neural Network (ANN), Naïve Bayes (NB), and Maximum Entropy (MaxEnt)—together with an Ensemble model, under identical geomorphological and environmental conditions. A GIS-based framework was applied using eleven conditioning factors derived from topographic, geological, hydrological, and land-cover datasets. A landslide inventory verified by field observations was used for model training and validation. Model performance was assessed using Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) analysis and the Area Under the Curve (AUC). All models achieved high predictive accuracy (AUC = 0.877–0.959). The NB model performed best (AUC = 0.959), while the Ensemble model produced the most spatially consistent susceptibility patterns. High- and very high-susceptibility zones were consistently associated with steep slopes and weak lithological units. Comparative machine learning approaches provide reliable and transferable tools for regional landslide susceptibility assessment. The results highlight the importance of algorithm selection and ensemble strategies in susceptibility mapping.

papers.title: Investigation on an Improved SegFormer with Multi-Module Fusion for Landslide Recognition in Remote Sensing Images
papers.summary: Landslides pose severe threats to life and property, necessitating rapid and accurate identification for effective hazard assessment and emergency response. This study proposes an improved SegFormer model for precise landslide extraction from high-resolution remote sensing imagery. To address the limitations of existing segmentation methods in handling complex backgrounds and irregular boundaries, the proposed framework integrates several structural enhancements. These include a squeeze-and-excitation module to suppress background noise, an auxiliary edge-fusion branch to capture explicit boundary details, and an adaptive feature gating mechanism to refine feature representation. The model is trained using focal loss to mitigate class imbalance and employs a three-stage recognition process, culminating in post-processing with dense conditional random fields for boundary refinement. Herein, the experimental results on a dataset of 100 high-resolution satellite images demonstrate that this approach outperforms the classical U-Net architecture and traditional thresholding techniques. The model achieved an accuracy of 0.976, a precision of 0.918, a recall of 0.947, and an F1-score of 0.932. These findings confirm that the proposed method offers exceptional accuracy and robustness, providing an effective automated tool for large-scale landslide detection in complex terrain.

papers.title: Identification of Landslide-Prone Areas and Mitigation Measures along the Proposed Chaumala–Garbha Road, Kailali, Nepal
papers.source: Universal Technical Journal of Lumbini International Academy of Science and Technology
papers.summary: This study identifies landslide-prone sections and appropriate mitigation measures along the proposed Chaumala–Garbha Road, a 22.317 km alignment (Chainage 0+000–22+317) in Kailali and Doti districts, Sudurpashchim Province, Nepal. Primary data (field observation, GPS survey, landslide inventory and photographic documentation) and secondary data (DEM, geology, land use/land cover and rainfall) were compiled at 500 m chainage intervals (46 stations) within a 1 km road-corridor buffer. A GIS-based Analytical Hierarchy Process (AHP) integrating eight conditioning factors – slope, geology, rainfall, land use/land cover, drainage, road proximity, aspect and elevation – was used to derive factor weights (slope 31.2%, geology 20.1%, rainfall 14.6%, land use/land cover and road proximity 10.4% each, drainage 6.8%, elevation 3.9%, aspect 2.6%) with a consistency ratio of 1.3%, well within Saaty's acceptable limit. The resulting Landslide Susceptibility Index classified 11.9 km (53.6%) of the corridor as Moderate, 9.7 km (43.4%) as High and 0.7 km (3.0%) as Low susceptibility, with no, very low or very high sections. The longest continuous high-risk stretches occur at chainage 4+550–10+700, 11+450–13+400 and 17+250–18+600. Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) validation returned an Area Under the Curve of 0.81, indicating good predictive accuracy. Field investigation attributed recurring failures mainly to inadequate drainage, haphazard road excavation, over-steepened cut slopes (70–80° against the 34–45° recommended for sandy soil), absence of stabilization structures and deforestation, corroborated by a focus group discussion and an in-depth interview with local stakeholders. Structural measures (retaining walls, breast walls, gabion walls and rock bolting) are recommended for high-susceptibility sections, and non-structural measures (surface drains, slope trimming and bioengineering) for moderate- and low-susceptibility sections. Integrated multi-criteria decision analysis and bivariate statistical modeling for landslide susceptibility zonation in the northwestern Ethiopian highlands
papers.summary: Landslides represent a critical geo-environmental hazard in the Ethiopian highlands, specifically within the Telemt, Janamora, and Beyeda districts, where they frequently result in fatalities and the destruction of vital infrastructure and agricultural land. This study integrated Geographic Information Systems (GIS) and remote sensing data to perform landslide susceptibility mapping (LSM) using two distinct modeling approaches: the Frequency Ratio (FR) and the Analytical Hierarchy Process (AHP). A total of 140 data points (98 for training (70%) and 42 for testing (30%)) were considered for modeling and validation. Eleven geo-environmental conditioning factors: Slope, rainfall, lithology, density of lineaments, curvature, aspect, normalized difference vegetation index, land use/land cover, distance to drainage, drainage density, and soil were analyzed to evaluate their influence on landslide occurrence. According to the AHP model, 13.69% and 26.91% of the study area were classified as very high and high susceptibility zones, respectively. In comparison, the FR model identified 12.09% as very high and 23.78% as high susceptibility zones. Both models underscored that steep slopes, porphyritic basalt unit, high lineament density, proximity to drainage systems, and concave terrain curvature are the primary drivers of slope instability. Conversely, gentle slopes, sandstone unit, and dense vegetation cover were strongly associated with low-susceptibility regions. Model performance was validated using the Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve, yielding an Area Under the Curve (AUC) value of 0.812 for the AHP model and 0.793 for the FR model, alongside a prediction rate AUC value of 77.4% (0.774) for the AHP model and 70.4% for the FR model, confirming the predictive reliability of both methods. These results provide essential geospatial intelligence for policy-makers and stakeholders to guide disaster risk management, sustainable land-use planning, and targeted reha

papers.title: Beyond Vulnerability: Women’s Water Stewardship and Adaptive Agency in Climate-Vulnerable Bangladesh
papers.summary: Abstract In Bangladesh, the climate crisis manifests through acute water scarcity, which profoundly disrupts social reproduction, particularly for women. Using a Feminist Political Ecology (FPE) lens, this study explores women’s adaptive agency in daily water management practices at both household and community levels. The study was conducted in three climate-vulnerable regions of Bangladesh: Mongla (cyclone-prone coastal Bagerhat), Naogaon (drought-prone), and Cox’s Bazar (flash flood- and landslide-prone). The study employed a qualitative approach incorporating in-depth interviews with women and focus group discussions which complemented by non-participant observation. In addition, key informant interviews were conducted with local government representatives, government officials and NGO staff working on climate change adaptation to understand the institutional setting. Data were thematically analysed following six steps of the thematic analysis process. The results show that women play a crucial role as water stewards, using their traditional knowledge, social networks, and collective action to enhance household and community resilience in the face of climate uncertainty. However, formal governance institutions seldom recognize their contributions. The study therefore recommends that local water governance and the vital role of women’s traditional knowledge be recognized in policies, and that leadership for a gender-responsive adaptation framework to climate change be adopted.

papers.title: Understanding the propagation processes and driving mechanisms of meteorological, hydrological, and agricultural droughts in Xinjiang
papers.summary: Drought propagation among meteorological, hydrological, and agricultural systems poses significant challenges to water security and agricultural sustainability in arid regions. This study investigated the propagation mechanisms and driving factors of multi-type droughts in Xinjiang, China, using ERA5-Land reanalysis data (1990–2024) to derive the standardized precipitation index (SPI), standardized runoff index (SRI), and standardized soil moisture index (SSI). Wavelet coherence analysis (WTC), maximum Pearson correlation coefficient (MPCC), Copula-based modeling, and SHAP analysis were integrated to identify drought propagation pathways, response thresholds, and dominant drivers. Results showed that drought variability decreased with increasing timescales, whereas SSI exhibited stronger persistence, and the coherence among drought types strengthened at medium- and long-term scales. Agricultural drought responded to meteorological drought with an average lag of approximately 4 months, while hydrological drought exhibited delays of 3–7 months, with agricultural-to-hydrological drought propagation occurring after 2–3 months. Propagation thresholds ranged from −1.00 to −1.97 for meteorological-to-hydrological drought, −1.07 to −2.28 for meteorological-to-agricultural drought, and − 1.04 to −2.32 for agricultural-to-hydrological drought. Soil moisture emerged as a key regulator of drought evolution, while precipitation availability, runoff processes, and hydrothermal conditions jointly controlled drought variability and propagation. These findings provide a scientific basis for drought monitoring, early warning, and adaptive water resource management under climate change, supporting agricultural drought mitigation and regional disaster risk reduction. Practical implications This research systematically elucidates the propagation patterns, critical thresholds, and driving mechanisms of drought across meteorological, hydrological, and agricultural systems. papers.title: Causes and impact of the 2081 Flood of Sunkoshi River in Khurkot, Golanjor Rural Municipality, Sindhuli, Nepal
papers.source: Universal Technical Journal of Lumbini International Academy of Science and Technology
papers.summary: Nepal’s steep topography and monsoon-dominated climate make it highly vulnerable to floods and flash floods. In 2081 B.S., a catastrophic flash flood struck Khurkot, at the confluence of the Sunkoshi and Tamakoshi rivers in Golanjor Rural Municipality, Sindhuli, and affected more than 500 families. This study was done to find the natural and human-induced causes of the flood, its socio-economic, infrastructural and environmental impacts, and ways to reduce future risk. A mixed-methods design was used. A household questionnaire survey was carried out with 150 respondents, and 19 problems associated with the flood, together with their causes, effects and mitigation measures, were ranked using the Relative Importance Index (RII). Field observation, a focus group discussion with community members and an in-depth interview with a technical expert of the rural municipality were also carried out. The results show that the biggest problem is weak coordination in disaster response and relief distribution (RII 0.88), followed by destruction of roads and transportation network (RII 0.87), loss of agricultural land and crops (RII 0.86) and riverbank erosion causing land loss (RII 0.85), while illegal riverbed extraction was ranked lowest (RII 0.71). The strongest cause of weak coordination was the absence of a clear inter-agency command and communication protocol (RII 0.83). Heavy monsoon rainfall, uncontrolled extraction of sand and gravel, removal of riverbank vegetation and inadequate flood protection structures were found to be important causes behind many of the impacts. Field observation showed that nearly 90 percent of the cultivated land in the affected belt was inundated, buried or swept away. The study suggests a single disaster coordination authority, stronger embankments and flood-resilient roads and bridges, better drainage, regulation of riverbed extraction, riverbank bioengineering, and an early warning system with community preparedness training.

papers.title: Permafrost Monitoring in the Arctic Network of National Parklands
papers.summary: Permafrost underlies most of the Arctic Network and affects nearly everything in the arctic ecosystem, from soils and vegetation to water and wildlife. Permafrost is ground that doesn’t thaw in the summer due to a cold climate. Permafrost perches water near the surface, making soils wet and runoff fast. The striking polygonal patterned ground so characteristic of the arctic is due to permafrost. Ice can build up in the ground and then thaw, producing pits, ponds, lakes, and landslides. Many scientists believe that our climate is warming and permafrost will thaw; some think that permafrost thaw has already started. Thaw of permafrost could have many consequences, such as drainage of lakes, creation of new ponds, soil erosion, slumps, siltation of streams and lakes, release of greenhouse gasses, and changes in soil wetness and nutrient supplies. Citation: Swanson D. Permafrost Monitoring in the Arctic Network of National Parklands. 2010. National Park Service Leads: Dave Swanson Sponsors: National Park Service Arctic Network Inventory and Monitoring Program Publisher: National Park Service

Unravelling landslide susceptibility controls using machine learning and explainable AI in a tropical river basin of the Western Ghats, India
papers.summary: Landslide susceptibility assessment is essential for risk-informed land-use planning in humid tropical river basins, where intense monsoon rainfall, steep terrain and expanding human disturbance interact to destabilise slopes. This study develops an explainable Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM) framework for landslide susceptibility mapping in the Manimala River Basin, Kerala, India. A landslide inventory and twelve conditioning factors, including slope, rainfall, topographic wetness index, lineaments, streams, roads, curvature, lithology, soil, and land use/land cover (LU/LC), were used to develop the model. The dataset was divided into training and testing subsets using a 70:30 ratio, and model performance was evaluated using AUROC, precision–recall, and confusion-matrix-based metrics. The LightGBM model showed strong predictive performance, with an AUROC of 0.894 and an average precision of 0.878. Threshold-based validation yielded an accuracy of 0.833, precision of 0.864, sensitivity of 0.792, specificity of 0.875, and an F1-score of 0.826, indicating balanced classification of landslide and non-landslide samples. The susceptibility map revealed that high- and very high-susceptibility zones together occupy 5.69% of the basin, mainly concentrated in the eastern and north-eastern uplands along the Western Ghats, whereas 83.66% of the basin falls under the least susceptible class. SHAP-based explainability identified slope as the dominant control on landslide susceptibility, followed in relative importance by rainfall, topographic wetness index (TWI), and distance to lineaments. The proposed explainable framework provides both accurate susceptibility mapping and transparent geomorphic interpretation for climate-resilient local planning.

papers.title: Climate hazards, water insecurity, and menstrual-health capability deprivation among women and girls in Bangladesh
papers.summary: This dataset contains the R code, variable dictionary, coding notes, supplementary appendix, and aggregate results for the article "Climate hazards, water insecurity, and menstrual-health capability deprivation among women and girls in Bangladesh: a nationally representative, geospatially linked cross-sectional study" (Howlader MH, Moin MMH). The study analyses 61,527 women aged 15–49 years in the 2025 Bangladesh Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS7). An Alkire–Foster index of menstrual-health capability deprivation (seven indicators in four dimensions: material adequacy, privacy and dignity, functional participation, and bodily agency and care access) is related to household-reported climate hazards (flood, drought, cyclone or tidal surge, landslide), drinking-water insufficiency, and hazard-related toilet disruption. Methods include survey-weighted logistic regression, average marginal effects, a negative-control outcome, E-values, and geographic analyses (Moran's I, Getis–Ord Gi* hot spots, Fay–Herriot district estimates, MICS geospatial covariates, coastal-zone effect modification, and spatially smoothed models). Contents: - code/: R scripts (00–06 and run_all.R) that reproduce all tables and figures in the article and supplementary appendix. - data/: instructions for obtaining the input data (data not included). - docs/: supplementary appendix (PDF), variable dictionary, coding notes, and conceptual framework figure. - results/: tables (xlsx), figures (PNG, PDF), district-level estimates (GeoPackage), verification report, and R session information. The MICS7 microdata, cluster GPS coordinates, and geospatial covariates belong to the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics and UNICEF and cannot be redistributed; they are available free of charge to registered users at https://mics.unicef.org/surveys. District boundaries are available at https://data.humdata.org/dataset/cod-ab-bgd. Only aggregate, non-identifiable results are included in this dataset.

papers.title: Comparative Analysis of Geotextile-Reinforced Embankment Slope Stability Using the Bishop Method in GeoStudio SLOPE/W and Finite Element Analysis in PLAXIS 2D: A Case Study of the Klaten–Purwomartani Toll Road Project, Section 1, Package 1.2, STA 38+000
papers.summary: This study aims to analyze the stability of embankment slopes in the Klaten–Purwomartani Toll Road Construction Project Section 1Package 1.2 STA 38+000 by comparing the analysis results using GeoStudio SLOPE/W and PLAXIS 2D, as well as evaluating the effectiveness of geotextile reinforcement and verification using the Bishop method. The research data were obtained from independent laboratory testing of subgrade soil at depths of 1–3 m. The classification results indicate that the subgrade soil is dominated by clay and silt with different shear strength characteristics at each depth, while the embankment material is classified as loamy sand. The analysis without reinforcement shows that increasing embankment height and variations in loading conditions reduce the Safety Factor (SF) value, with the most critical condition occurring at an 8 m embankment height, which does not meet the requirements of SNI 8460:2017 (SF ≥ 1.5). The application of Woven Staple Fiber Polypropylene UNW-60P geotextile reinforcement effectively increases the SF value by approximately 80%, allowing all critical conditions to meet the stability requirements. Verification using the Bishop method produces SF values ranging from 1.626–2.884, all of which satisfy the requirements of SNI 8460:2017. The comparative analysis results show that PLAXIS 2D produces more conservative SF values because it considers stress distribution, deformation, and pore water pressure using the Finite Element Method (FEM) with the Strength Reduction Method (SRM), while GeoStudio SLOPE/W based on the Limit Equilibrium Method (LEM) produces relatively higher SF values and is suitable for preliminary slope stability evaluation.

papers.title: Ecological Indicators Reveal Contrasting Post-Earthquake Recovery Trajectories and Resilience Across Mountain Ecosystems
papers.summary: Net primary productivity (NPP) is a useful ecological indicator for evaluating ecosystem functioning and recovery after natural disturbance. Here, we used multi-source remote-sensing and environmental data from 2010 to 2024 to compare post-earthquake NPP recovery in the 2017 Jiuzhaigou and Milin earthquake regions. We integrated trend analysis, temporal persistence assessment, co-seismic landslide overlay, eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) interpreted using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP), and locally weighted scatterplot smoothing (LOWESS)-based contribution-transition detection to compare NPP dynamics and environmental associations in the two earthquake-affected regions. The two regions exhibited contrasting responses. The slope of regional mean annual NPP decreased from 9.69 to 8.21 g C m−2 yr−2 between the pre- and post-earthquake periods in Jiuzhaigou, whereas it increased from 3.69 to 9.37 g C m−2 yr−2 in Milin. Hurst-based trend-persistence analysis indicated a higher proportion of sustained improvement and a lower proportion of degradation-related classes in Jiuzhaigou, whereas Milin showed more degradation-related classes. Within co-seismic landslide zones, sustained degradation dominated in both regions and was more extensive in Milin. XGBoost–SHAP results showed that pre-earthquake NPP was the most influential predictor in both regions, but the contributions of secondary predictors differed. Elevation made a larger relative contribution to the Jiuzhaigou model, whereas pre-earthquake NDVI, precipitation, and temperature made larger relative contributions to the Milin model. LOWESS analysis further revealed distinct nonlinear response transitions in temperature, precipitation, and elevation. These results demonstrate the value of combining NPP trends, temporal persistence, and model interpretation to compare vegetation productivity dynamics and inform assessments of post-earthquake functional recovery in mountain ecosystems.

papers.title: Use of bamboo-based bio-engineering for flood and soil erosion control: a case study of Jhiku Khola, Kavrepalanchok District, Nepal
papers.source: Universal Technical Journal of Lumbini International Academy of Science and Technology
papers.summary: Floods and soil erosion along mid-hill streams severely threaten agricultural land, infrastructure and rural livelihoods across Nepal. While conventional civil engineering structures such as gabions and masonry walls involve high capital and maintenance costs, bamboo-based soil bio-engineering offers a sustainable, nature-based alternative. This study evaluates the application, perceived effectiveness and operational constraints of bamboo bio-engineering along the Jhiku Khola in Panchkhal Municipality, Kavrepalanchok District. Using a mixed-method approach, primary data were gathered between March and August 2020 through a structured questionnaire survey (n = 108) analyzed with the Relative Importance Index (RII), complemented by focus group discussions, key informant interviews and field observations. Floods (RII = 0.77), concentrated in the monsoon, and soil erosion (RII = 0.69) were identified as major hazards, with loss of agricultural land (RII = 0.81) cited as the most serious problem. Although 91% of respondents recognized the utility of bamboo in flood mitigation, only 63% had implemented it, highlighting a critical execution gap. Bamboo bio-engineering was rated highly effective (RII = 0.71) and emerged as the most preferred solution (RII = 0.81), with Bansi, Choya and Nigalo identified as the most suitable local species. The main implementation hurdles were a shortage of technical, site-specific studies and designs, weak inter-governmental coordination and the difficulty of transporting bamboo to the river basin; these are compounded by the absence of municipal rate analysis norms for bio-engineering items and by seasonal constraints on budget release, planting material and labour. The study underscores the need to integrate hybrid bio-engineering, combining gabion or masonry toe protection with vegetative palisades, into local disaster risk reduction plans and public procurement frameworks.

papers.title: Study on problems associated with reactive maintenance of roads: A case of selected highways in Far-Western Nepal
papers.source: Universal Technical Journal of Lumbini International Academy of Science and Technology
papers.summary: Road maintenance in the mid-hills and high hills of far-western Nepal is largely reactive, where interventions are made only after pavements, slopes and drainage structures have already failed. Such practice restores traffic temporarily but increases long-term cost and shortens the service life of roads, and very few studies have been carried out to find its root causes in the region. Hence, this study was conducted with an aim to assess the major problems, causes and effects of reactive maintenance of roads and to draw effective mitigation measures for the Khodpe-Chainpur Highway (NH-64), Satbanjh-Gokuleshwor-Darchula section of Mahakali Highway (NH-66) and Anarkholi-Jhulaghat section of Mid-Hill Highway (NH-03). Primary data were collected through field observation, in-depth interview, focus group discussion and questionnaire survey, whereas secondary data were collected from published journal articles, theses, government databases and annual reports. The data collected from 130 respondents were analyzed in Excel using the Relative Importance Index (RII) for Likert scale questions. The results showed that the major problem is escalating structural and geotechnical failures with the highest RII value of 0.80, followed by destruction of supporting works along the road and emergency cleaning of landslides and rockfalls (RII 0.78). Unmanaged vulnerable and unstable slopes, no maintenance of deformed retaining walls until they collapse, limited budget for periodic maintenance and the practice of awarding contracts to the lowest financial bid were identified as the main causes. Among the effects, cyclical budget exhaustion and repeated maintenance received the highest RII of 0.84, indicating that repeated emergency interventions impose a substantial financial burden on road authorities. Dataset of DInSAR wrapped phase signals for AI-based automated detection and classification of mass movements
papers.summary: Abstract With the growing use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in remote sensing of mass movements, open and suitable datasets for model training and validation are increasingly needed. Although Differential Synthetic Aperture Radar Interferometry (DInSAR) is a widely used technique for studying mass movements, wrapped interferograms remain less exploited, and the importance of geomorphological expertise in their interpretation is not usually emphasised. In this work, we introduce a dataset of DInSAR wrapped phase signals designed to support the development of Deep Learning (DL) models for the automated detection and classification of active slow-moving mass movements. The dataset covers two selected wide areas in the Central European Alps and the Northern Apennines. It contains 4910 expert-annotated DInSAR wrapped phase signals derived from 92 Sentinel-1 interferograms with temporal baselines ranging from 6 days to 1 year, classified into nine distinct landslide and periglacial landform classes after careful geomorphological interpretation. This dataset is expected to support the scientific community in AI-based applications for mass movement research, while also serving as a benchmark for the generation of comparable datasets.

papers.title: Dynamic fusion of displacement parallelism and mass conservation for landslide slip-surface depth inversion from SBAS-InSAR observations: a case study in the Wudongde reservoir area
Assessing Natural Hazard Exposure and Demographic Vulnerability in Serbian LSGUs Using FAHP and FMULTIMOORA
papers.summary: Natural hazards increasingly represent a significant challenge to sustainable development, disaster risk reduction, and population wellbeing, particularly in regions affected by adverse demographic trends. This study examines the interaction between natural hazard exposure and demographic vulnerability across 25 Serbian local self-government units (LSGUs) through the integration of Geographic Information Systems (GIS), the Triangular Fuzzy Analytic Hierarchy Process (FAHP), and the Fuzzy MULTIMOORA method. Fifteen indicators were organized into three groups representing natural hazard exposure, hazard exposure within built-up areas, and demographic vulnerability. The hazard-related indicators included flood-prone areas, landslide and rockfall susceptibility, seismic hazard, hail-prone areas, and areas exposed to erosion and torrential floods. The demographic indicators included the shares of people with disabilities, population aged 65 years and over, population without educational attainment, economically inactive population, and elderly single-person households. Criterion weights were determined using Triangular FAHP, while Fuzzy MULTIMOORA was applied to rank LSGUs according to their integrated vulnerability. Additional group-specific Fuzzy MULTIMOORA analyses were conducted separately for each indicator group to identify the principal drivers of vulnerability. The integrated assessment identified Ljubovija, Vladičin Han, and Krupanj as the most vulnerable LSGUs, whereas Lebane, Gadžin Han, and Vladimirci occupied the lowest positions. papers.title: Study on the geo-environmental and socio-economic impacts of tunnelling works in fragile Himalayan geology: a case study of Nagdhunga Tunnel, Dahachowk, Nepal
papers.source: Universal Technical Journal of Lumbini International Academy of Science and Technology
papers.summary: Tunnelling in the fragile geological formations of the Nepalese Himalayas presents complex geotechnical, hydrogeological and socio-economic challenges. The Nagdhunga–Sisnekhola Tunnel Road Project, Nepal’s first major highway traffic tunnel, was initiated to bypass the congested Sisnekhola–Thankot loop. However, sub-surface excavation has induced significant ground deformation and hydrological disruptions in overlying settlements. This study evaluates the localized environmental, structural and socio-economic impacts of tunnel construction on the Dahachowk area (Ward No. 1) of Chandragiri Municipality, Kathmandu. Utilizing a mixed-method design, primary empirical data were gathered through a household survey (n = 156) analyzed via the Relative Importance Index (RII), supplemented by field observations of 42 dug wells, 12 key informant interviews and 3 focus group discussions. Structural cracks and building damage emerged as the most severe impact (RII = 0.91), followed closely by slope instability/landslides and the drying of traditional drinking water sources (RII = 0.89). Hydrogeological analysis revealed that sub-surface water drawdown significantly lowered pore water pressure, triggering ground settlement, sinkhole formation (RII = 0.91) and building tilt, particularly along the shallow eastern portal zone. The depletion of natural springs increased financial burdens and disproportionately heightened the water-fetching burden on women and children. Furthermore, the absence of a pre-construction Pre-Condition Survey (PCS) and an inaccessible Grievance Redress Mechanism (GRM) exacerbated community distrust, prompting formal complaints to the project financier (JICA). The study recommends mandatory pre-condition structural surveys, pre-excavation grouting, real-time piezometric monitoring, independent third-party damage assessments and community-managed water supply restoration for future tunnelling projects in Nepal.

papers.title: Evolution of Erosional Badlands in the Eastern Black Sea Region During the Late Holocene
papers.summary: This paper presents the results of geomorphological research conducted in the Mussera Upland (Western Abkhazia) in 2024. Based on morphometric analysis and geomorphological survey within the typical river basin (Ryapsh River basin), the topographical features of the upland were described in detail, and radiocarbon dating of alluvial deposits was performed. We found that the Mussera Upland is a typical humid badland with a dissection density of 3–4 km/km 2 . The formation of a low-order fluvial network begins here within a catchment area of approximately 0.01 km 2 . Within the dendritic catchment of the Ryapsh River, erosional slopes of varying steepness cover 94% of the total area, with only about 6% occupied by alluvial terraces in the valley floor (up to 1.5 m and up to 3.0 m above the riverbed). Both of these terraces were formed during the Holocene within the last thousand years: the low alluvial level formed no earlier than 570–670 cal yr BP, and the upper alluvial level in the Ryapsh River valley was formed about 810–960 cal yr BP. The development of the Mussera badland is occurring with the leading role of erosional and slope processes (primarily landslides) under conditions of ongoing tectonic uplift. The forest cover of the area does not prevent slope denudation, but, instead, it often triggers it. The development of the badland is characterized by two opposing trends: over time, the ridges are lowered due to slope denudation; however the depth of dissection does not decrease due to ongoing tectonic uplift and active stream downcutting. In recent decades climate change has increased the frequency of extreme rainfall events, resulting in a noticeable rise in denudation rates.

papers.title: Pysammos 1.0.0: a discrete-to-continuum transformation Python tool to analyse the rheology of granular materials
papers.summary: Abstract. Granular flow processes involving different interstitial fluids and coupling regimes are widespread in both natural systems (e.g., landslides, rock avalanches, river sediment transport) and industrial applications (e.g., aggregates in concrete manufacturing, powder technology, animal feed). Despite this, the behaviour of complex granular flows is not fully understood. Modelling of granular media through software packages that couple the Discrete Element Method with Computational Fluid Dynamics (DEM-CFD) enables a comprehensive description of granular small-scale mechanics through simulations of particle-particle and particle-fluid interactions at high temporal and spatial resolution. These approaches are pivotal in the development of constitutive models that represent the bulk rheology of granular media. While DEM-CFD simulations provide particle-scale information (e.g., particle velocities and forces), extracting continuum fields requires a discrete-to-continuum (D2C) transformation that applies a mathematical approach termed coarse-graining. Although some DEM software packages include built-in D2C capabilities, others, such as MFiX-DEM, do not. Consequently, users are often required to develop custom D2C workflows or adapt simulation outputs to the requirements of other D2C tools. Hence, we introduce Pysammos, a Python package that performs discrete-to-continuum transformations and is designed to be user-friendly, open-source, and computationally efficient. Pysammos is able to process polydisperse granular mixtures of any particle shape, while also offering the option to analyse different particle phases separately. It post-processes output files from MFiX-DEM software and produces vtkhdf outputs ready for visualisation in ParaView, as well as a more generic h5 format for further data analysis. Pysammos is able to operate on standard desktop computers as well as on HPC systems. Finally, we showcase a variety of exemplar applications such as sediment eros

papers.summary: Rainfall-induced landslides along Malaysian highway cut slopes are commonly evaluated using empirical thresholds, with limited consideration of cumulative antecedent rainfall. This study evaluates a machine-learning rainfall threshold for five documented shallow-slope failures along Federal Route FT185 (Jalan Simpang Pulai–Blue Valley), Perak, Malaysia, using 520 site-days of daily rainfall records. Cumulative rainfall was calculated over seven windows (1, 3, 5, 7, 14, 21 and 30 days), together with a short-burst intensity feature and a wet-day count and six classifiers (logistic regression, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, k-nearest neighbours, a support vector machine and XGBoost) were trained under class-weighted, leave-one-site-out cross-validation. Random Forest achieved the best discrimination (ROC-AUC = 0.817), with 80% sensitivity and 90% specificity. Antecedent rainfall consistently ranked above same-day rainfall, indicating the importance of longer-duration rainfall accumulation in the present dataset. An interpretable two-feature logistic regression boundary (14-day antecedent rainfall vs. same-day rainfall) and Random Forest partial-dependence saturation points (approximately 203, 330 and 447 mm for the 14-, 21- and 30-day windows) were derived and combined into a two-tier watch/warning rainfall-probability threshold. The results provide preliminary, site-specific rainfall thresholds for the investigated corridor within a pilot methodological framework requiring prospective validation with additional independent failure events before operational application.

The projects explore how architectural design can respond to environmental risks while maintaining practical and functional living conditions. The study aims to develop an understanding of practical and affordable architectural approaches that may contribute to safer residential environments in vulnerable areas of Bangladesh.

papers.title: Analysis of amplifying effect of antecedent drought on rainfall-induced shallow landslides
papers.summary: Abstract Rainfall-induced shallow landslides are typically attributed to short-term meteorological triggers such as rainfall intensity and duration. However, the influence of antecedent hydrological conditions, particularly prolonged dry spells, has received limited attention despite their potential to alter soil behavior significantly. This study investigates the role of antecedent dry spells on landslide occurrence in the clay-rich terrains of the eastern Black Sea region of Türkiye. Four intense rainfall events from two study sites were examined. At both sites, the later event followed a prolonged dry period and produced a substantially larger mapped landslide inventory despite lower landslide-day rainfall than the earlier event, which occurred under wetter antecedent conditions. To investigate the mechanisms underlying this behavior and evaluate whether it was evident across the event inventories, we combined mechanistic numerical simulations with a data-driven statistical analysis. Numerical simulations indicate that a configuration representing crack-related hydraulic and mechanical changes enhances infiltration and reduces matric suction, resulting in strength reduction and lower slope stability. Additionally, a Generalized Additive Model incorporating landslide-day precipitation, the 30-day Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI-30), local relief, slope steepness, and aspect reveals that landslides are more likely to occur when intense rainfall coincides with drier antecedent conditions rather than under persistently wet conditions. The model showed consistent discriminatory performance under grouped tenfold cross-validation, with an overall ROC AUC of 0.836 based on combined validation-fold predictions. These findings suggest that in clay-rich environments, conventional rainfall thresholds used in predictive models may underestimate landslide occurrence probability when preceded by dry spells. papers.summary: A digital twin in mining is a dynamic, real-time virtual representation of physical assets and operational processes that supports predictive modeling, optimization, and decision-making. This chapter examines the architecture, data integration strategies, modeling approaches, and practical applications of digital twins in geotechnical monitoring within mining environments. It outlines the concept of digital twins and their key advantages, including improved operational efficiency, enhanced safety, and increased sustainability. Core components of a digital twin include data layers such as sensor streams, geospatial information systems, and engineering models alongside integration frameworks based on application programming interfaces and modular services, as well as visualization tools such as 3D environments, dashboards, and immersive technologies. Data ingestion encompasses both real-time monitoring sources, including advanced sensing systems, and historical datasets. Modeling approaches are categorized into physics-based methods, data-driven techniques, and hybrid models that combine both paradigms. Digital twins enable a range of use cases, including predictive analysis of slope stability, monitoring of tailings storage facilities, optimization of ventilation systems, tracking of infrastructure deformation, and support for emergency response planning. This chapter addresses real-time analytics pipelines that incorporate streaming architectures, edge computing, and operationalized machine learning, and covers key considerations for model validation, uncertainty quantification, and data governance. Illustrative examples demonstrate practical implementation concepts, supported by comparative analyses of system architectures, latency considerations, and sensor network configurations. Case studies from mining operations highlight applications such as slope failure monitoring, tailings surveillance, integrated mine-wide digital twins, and emergency response scenarios.

papers.summary: ABSTRACT This study evaluates andesite rock slope stability in İzmir, Türkiye, using mobile LiDAR (iPhone 14Pro) and hybrid classification systems. The acquired 3D point cloud (1.7 × 106 points) demonstrated high spatial accuracy when validated against global navigation satellite system data. Automated analysis via discontinuity set extractor revealed that applying a “full-persistence” assumption artificially reduces mean discontinuity spacing by 40–70 percent compared with a realistic “non-persistence” model, drastically underestimating rock block sizes. Kinematic analysis indicated a 40 percent probability of wedge failure, primarily driven by the highly persistent J6 set (lmax = 16 m). To directly compare slope mass rating (SMR), Q-slope, and rock hazard index (RHI) outputs, a “normalized risk index (Rindex)” was utilized. SMR yielded an overly optimistic evaluation Rindex = 0.41, failing to capture the geometric severity of the critical wedge. In contrast, RHI successfully identified this localized hazard (“moderate risk,” Rindex = 0.51) by directly accounting for geometric continuity. The Q-slope system proved to be the most conservative (Rindex = 0.60), indicating that the current 72° slope requires a reduction to 57°. The findings demonstrate that integrating mobile LiDAR with geometry-sensitive systems such as RHI provides a more reliable, targeted hazard assessment than traditional approaches.

papers.title: Shear-Performance Analysis of Piezoelectric Anchors in Rock-Slope Monitoring
papers.summary: ABSTRACT Bolt-stress monitoring is essential for rock-slope stability, yet conventional methods often fail to capture internal stress evolution and shear-surface locations. This study develops a piezoelectric anchor integrated with a self-sensing piezoelectric geotechnical cable (SPGC). Static-load double-shear tests were conducted under different shear-plane distances and rates. The SPGC voltage response correlated strongly with shear displacement, and the maximum monitored strain reached 6.34 %. Under the tested single-shear-plane conditions, the relative impedance and voltage responses identified the vicinity of the prescribed shear plane. Within 0.2–25 mm/min, effective voltage followed power-law relationships with R2 values of 0.98–0.99, whereas peak voltage followed exponential relationships with R2 values of 0.94–0.99. This research verifies the feasibility of using piezoelectric anchors to invert the depth and rate of rock mass slip, providing robust technical support for distributed dynamic monitoring and disaster early warning in geotechnical engineering.

papers.summary: Soil water infiltration (SWI) is central to hydrology and erosion assessment, but the measurement method and surface condition may affect the rates obtained. We compared a double-ring infiltrometer (DRI) with a rainfall simulator (InfiAsper) on a Dystric Acrisol with a sandy clay loam A horizon, under bare tilled soil and under maize straw. InfiAsper applied five rainfall treatments of equal erosivity, combining intensities of 44.6–75.0 mm h−1 with durations of 106–38 min, on four to five plots per treatment and surface. DRI tests were carried out in the same fields (22 under bare soil, 13 under ground cover) and analysed as an independent group. We (i) determined the final infiltration rate (SIR_f), (ii) compared DRI with InfiAsper, and (iii) evaluated the Kostiakov–Lewis, Horton and Philip models. Under bare soil, InfiAsper means ranged from 21.6 to 37.7 mm h−1 and the DRI mean was 86 mm h−1. A planned contrast between DRI and the mean of the five InfiAsper treatments gave a DRI/InfiAsper ratio of 1.80 (95% CI 1.00–3.23; p = 0.049); with the 20 tests of at least 15 readings, it was 2.13 (1.22–3.71). papers.title: Theory of Recession Based on Concepts from Percolation Theory
papers.summary: Abstract. Using the definition of recession as the decline in streamflow following a rainfall event peak and before the next peak (provided evapotranspiration may be neglected), recession defines the relationship between catchment storage and outflow. The present analysis addresses the limiting processes absent in existing recession analysis, which are nonetheless treatable in the language of percolation theory. This includes: a) a universal decline in hydraulic conductivity as the percolation threshold is approached, and b) a universal decline in accessible moisture content beyond the simple decline in overall moisture content. The process of addressing these two time-dependent phenomena generates the basic structure of recession response: 1) linear response for an average of multiple events, 2) the corresponding time frame variation, 3) the specific characteristics of its non-linear response, specifically, its convexity. The present approach results in an absolute value of the non-linearity that is still underestimated as compared to results published in the literature.

papers.summary: Groundwater plays a critical role in sustaining the ecological integrity and water security of the Chalan Beel, the largest inland wetland (5097 km2) in the Lower Atrai River Basin of northwestern Bangladesh. This study delineates groundwater potential zones (GWPZs) using an integrated Geographic Information System (GIS), Remote Sensing (RS), and Analytical Hierarchy Process (AHP) approach. Seventeen hydrogeological, topographic, climatic, and environmental thematic layers, including rainfall, soil type, soil permeability, groundwater level, aquifer depth, land use/land cover, geomorphology, drainage density, NDVI, and NDWI, were analyzed to evaluate groundwater recharge and storage potential. The AHP results indicate that rainfall (20%), soil type (16%), and soil permeability (13%) are the most influential factors controlling groundwater occurrence and recharge. The generated GWPZ map classified the study area into three categories: very high (65 km2, 1%), medium (3933 km2, 77%), and low (1099 km2, 22%) potential zones. Temporal NDVI analysis (1990–2024) revealed substantial changes in vegetation and moisture conditions, with the moderate NDVI class increasing from 45 to 67%, indicating improved vegetation cover and its strong association with groundwater recharge potential. The identified high- and moderate-potential zones provide important information for groundwater development, irrigation planning, and ecosystem conservation. The study offers a scientific basis for sustainable groundwater-dependent ecosystem (SGDE) management and supports informed decision-making for water-resource planning under increasing climatic variability and anthropogenic pressures in northwestern Bangladesh.

papers.title: From wetting-front coalescence to urban road collapse: interpretable machine learning of hydro-mechanical failure under coupled rainfall and pipeline leakage
papers.summary: Abstract Urban ground collapse poses a severe threat to public safety, road operation and underground infrastructure in densely developed cities. This study investigates the hydro-mechanical failure mechanism of road collapse induced by coupled rainfall infiltration and pipeline leakage through physical model testing, finite element simulation and interpretable surrogate modelling. A validated numerical model incorporating saturation-dependent strength and stiffness degradation was used to generate 120 cases with different pipe burial depths, rainfall intensities and leakage pressures.The results indicate that collapse develops through shallow-soil pre-wetting, leakage-induced wetting-zone expansion, convergence of the upper and lower wetting fronts, and upward propagation of deformation. Leakage pressure is the dominant factor, contributing 86.42%, 87.79% and 92.77% to the variations in collapse depth, near-saturated zone area and wetting-front depth, respectively. Rainfall mainly dissipates matric suction and lowers the failure threshold, whereas burial depth regulates the wetting-front convergence and deformation-transfer path. GPR/Kriging achieved test-set (R 2 ) values of 0.997–0.998, while XGBoost-SHAP confirmed the mechanism of leakage-pressure domination, rainfall amplification and burial-depth regulation. Risk zoning further shows that increasing rainfall shifts high-risk conditions towards lower leakage pressures, particularly at intermediate burial depths. The proposed framework provides an efficient tool for identifying vulnerable pipeline sections and supporting targeted inspection and collapse prevention.

Machine learning (ML) models are being trained on sewer inspection data to perform as modern asset-management tools.
