Tracer-based infiltration estimates are one such indicator. To our knowledge, this is the first study to combine these two techniques and compare ML-based structural failure probability with independent tracer-based evidence of groundwater infiltration under dry-weather conditions. As infiltration cannot be reliably estimated at the pipe level, we aggregated the studied network into 21 operational zones and estimated infiltration severity using dry-weather tracer data, based on electrical conductivity (EC) and chemical oxygen demand (COD), within a binary mixing framework. In parallel, ML-based condition prediction models were developed using an IPCW-weighted machine-learning framework trained on CCTV inspection data, aggregating the resulting predicted failure probabilities to the zone level using length-weighted averaging. Zones were ranked according to ML-predicted failure probability and tracer-based infiltration severity. The agreement between the two rankings was positive but statistically uncertain (Kendall's τ-b = 0.254-0.305; p = 0.108-0.056; concordance index = 0.628-0.655). Overall, the proposed framework provides a practical cross-evidence screening approach for environmental management and sewer asset-management decision-making when comprehensive inspection data are unavailable.

papers.title: Evaluating pre- and post-failure behavior of a large waste dump by combining LEM and DEM approach: a case study from a hydropower station, China
papers.summary: Large hydropower projects generate extensive waste dumps, posing significant environmental risks. Conventional 2D analyses fail to capture 3D topographic effects of typical gully terrain, while 3D discrete element method (DEM) are suitable but face calibration challenges for post-failure simulations. This study investigates a waste dump at the Yongjia Pumped Storage Power Station, China by integrating (1) a self-developed rigorous 3D Limit Equilibrium Method (LEM) for the pre-failure analysis and (2) a well-calibrated DEM for post-failure behavior. The 3D LEM reveals how meandering topography enhances stability, underscoring 3D analysis necessity. DEM simulations identify the interparticle friction coefficient (μ) as the controlling factor for debris flow trajectories and deposition patterns in winding valleys. A key highlight lies in the qualitative cross-model comparison linking the pre-failure and post-failure analyses, which supports μ = 0.2 as a representative value for the present DEM configuration and the engineering scenarios considered. This leads to a local mobilized area that remains confined within proximal slopes in DEM simulations, equivalent to a slight stability margin in LEM from the same local topographic constraints. However, failure risks persist under extreme conditions (e.g., drainage failure), where strength parameter uncertainties may arise from inadequate compaction or water lubrication (further reducing μ). Our cross-model results suggest specific reinforcement strategies to reduce the downstream risk.

papers.title: Spatial associations between urbanization, watershed runoff potential, and groundwater-depth change in a Semi-Arid Alluvial Plain, Multan, Pakistan
papers.summary: Groundwater decline in irrigated semi-arid alluvial plains reflects interacting land-surface, climatic, pumping, and hydrogeological controls. This study evaluates spatial associations among urbanization, Curve Number-based event-runoff potential, regional climate variability, and groundwater-depth change in Multan, Pakistan. Thirty-nine wells with pre- and post-monsoon observations for 2005, 2010, 2015, and 2018 were assigned to four watershed groups delineated using an approximately 30-m DEM and HydroBASINS Level-12 topology. Land-use/land-cover maps for 2010, 2015, and 2020, SoilGrids Hydrologic Soil Group data, and regional NASA POWER climate data for 2003–2018 were summarized using the same watershed boundaries. Mean groundwater-depth increases from pre-monsoon 2005 to post-monsoon 2018 were 19.32, 7.21, 5.76, and 15.69 m in Groups 1–4, respectively. Only Group 1 had a 95% confidence interval excluding zero. Urban fraction increased in all groups, while mean Curve Number values remained high and increased modestly by 0.24–0.64. Scenario calculations indicated only modest changes in event runoff. Climate analysis showed modest spatial rainfall variability, no significant trends in precipitation, temperature, or reference evapotranspiration, and no significant exploratory climate–groundwater relationship. The non-monotonic group patterns indicate that the available land-surface and climate indicators cannot independently explain the observed groundwater changes. The framework identifies priority areas for additional hydrogeological monitoring and management.

papers.title: Fractal and multifractal characteristics of particle-size distributions in debris-flow deposits
papers.summary: Particle-size distribution is a fundamental characteristic of debris-flow deposits and provides important information on sediment transport, sorting, and depositional processes. This study investigates ten debris-flow deposit profiles along the sampled main-channel reach along Jiangjiagou, Yunnan Province, China. Mechanical sieving combined with laser diffraction was employed to obtain high-resolution particle-size data, and single-fractal and multifractal approaches were used to quantitatively characterize the spatial variability, structural complexity, and multiscale heterogeneity of particle-size distributions. The results reveal that the deposits were dominated by the coarse fraction (> 0.05 mm), which accounted for 95.75–99.82% of the total particle-size composition, whereas clay and silt contents varied among sampling sites, indicating clear spatial differentiation in particle-size organization. The global fractal dimension ranges from 2.09 to 2.40, reflecting substantial variability in particle mixing and granulometric complexity. The generalized dimension spectra exhibit a typical inverted S-shaped pattern, while D₀, D₁, and D₂ show marked spatial variations among sampling sites. The characteristic singularity strength (α₀) ranges from 0.768 to 1.714, and the spectrum width (Δα) varies from 1.19 to 2.49. D₁/D₀ values are consistently well below unity, further indicating pronounced heterogeneity and multiscale variability in particle-size distributions. Correlation analysis shows that the fractal and multifractal characteristics are closely related to particle-size composition, with fine-particle enrichment generally associated with higher granulometric complexity, whereas coarser deposits tend to exhibit relatively simplified fractal structures. These results demonstrate that fractal and multifractal parameters provide an effective quantitative framework for characterizing the complex particle-size architecture of debris-flow deposits and offer new insights

papers.title: Interplay of fabric anisotropy and drainage direction in soil–water retention behaviour of sand-silt mixtures
papers.summary: The soil–water retention curve (SWRC) is commonly treated as a material function in unsaturated soil analyses, although it may be affected by soil fabric and the drainage boundary condition imposed during laboratory testing. This study employs a coupled Discrete Element Method–Pore Network Model (DEM–PNM) framework to investigate the combined influence of fabric anisotropy and drainage direction on the water-retention behaviour of sand-silt mixtures. The model is first verified against experimental SWRCs reported for specimens subjected to different stress ratios. A systematic numerical program is then conducted on seven sand-silt mixtures with different grain-size distributions and three relative densities. Cylindrical specimens are prepared under different triaxial stress ratios to generate different stress-induced fabric states and pore-network anisotropy. Drying SWRCs are then simulated under three drainage configurations: one-dimensional bottom drainage, bottom-plus-lateral drainage, and full all-directional drainage. The results show that the pore-size distribution index, λ, remains largely insensitive to stress ratio and drainage condition. In contrast, the air-entry value (AEV) is affected by fabric anisotropy when drainage is restricted to a one-dimensional path, particularly when the major principal stress direction during specimen preparation is aligned with the drainage direction, a configuration commonly encountered in laboratory SWRC tests. For the lateral or full all-directional drainage configurations, numerical simulations indicate the effect of stress-induced anisotropy becomes negligible, as air invasion is governed by the most accessible boundary-connected pore pathways. Accordingly, a simple correction model is proposed to account for drainage-dependent AEV variation. Tracing soil–water signatures from contrasting land uses in low-flow streamwater of a mixed headwater catchment
papers.summary: Baseflow sustains water delivery from headwater catchments during non-event conditions and low flows. However, in mixed land-use headwater catchments, how land-use-related soil–water storage signatures are represented in low-flow streamwater and vary seasonally remain poorly understood. To address this gap, a two-year study involving monthly monitoring of a hilly purple-soil headwater catchment was conducted. We employed a combination of dissolved organic matter (DOM) fluorescence, stable water isotopes, and Bayesian mixing analysis to characterize source composition in low-flow streamwater, characterize temporal variation in dominant source signatures, and assess depth-related soil–water signatures under baseflow-dominated conditions. This study showed that orchard, sloping farmland, and paddy soil waters formed the main source-signature group, with a summed mean posterior attribution of 62.9% across the 19 retained samples, and summed monthly posterior-median attributions ranging from 52.7% to 72.8%, compared with a mean attribution of 10.7% to sampled valley shallow groundwater (monthly posterior-median range: 4.7%-26.1%). The dominant-source pattern showed seasonal variation among orchard, sloping farmland, and paddy soil waters, with estimated layer attributions favoring shallow layers (10 cm) in orchard and sloping farmland and middle layers (20–30 cm) in paddy; exploratory analyses indicated associations with bulk density and DOC. The findings indicate that different land-use types are associated with distinct soil–water storage signatures in low-flow streamwater, providing a basis for evaluating how future land-use changes may influence low-flow hydrological functioning.

papers.title: Seasonal variability of total streamflow, runoff, baseflow, and baseflow index in the fetam catchment, Upper Blue Nile Basin, Ethiopia
papers.summary: Groundwater is often a primary source of freshwater in many parts of the world. Fetam River Catchment is among the major river catchments in Ethiopia’s Upper Blue Nile River Basin, where groundwater is a primary source of freshwater. Seasonal rainfall fluctuations, climate, and anthropogenic factors strongly influence the quantity and quality of surface water. Therefore, estimating groundwater recharge is essential for understanding aquifer dynamics and provides a critical basis for sustainable groundwater management. The main aim of the investigation is to estimate the amount of water recharged to the aquifer using the soil moisture balance and Baseflow separation methods in the Fetam River Catchment, and to determine water management thresholds for sustainable development. Fifteen years of River flow data and ten years of daily meteorological data have been used for Baseflow separation and daily soil moisture balance, respectively. Daily soil moisture data analysis yielded a recharge rate of 253.1 ± 78 mm/year, and time-series baseflow data yielded a recharge rate of 187.5 ± 13.23 mm/year. Therefore, the average recharge rate of the catchment based on the two recharge estimation techniques is 220 ± 45.6 mm/year, a sufficient renewable resource. Despite the effects of numerous factors, Baseflow resulted in an underestimation, and the soil moisture balance is overestimated in the investigated area compared to the average of the two techniques. Therefore, the recharge value for river catchments under similar geographical and meteorological circumstances is better estimated by the average of all methods than by any individual technique.

papers.title: Evaluation of Pervious Concrete Pavement for Phreatic Groundwater Recharge: https://doi.org/10.46610/JoCCS.2026.v011i03.004
papers.source: Journal of Ceramics and Concrete Sciences
papers.summary: The amount of impervious surfaces associated with urban development has increased, altering the natural flow of rainwater and reducing the amount of rainfall that can infiltrate into the ground. Concrete and bituminous roads also tend to direct much of the rainfall into the drainage system, thereby increasing surface runoff and reducing groundwater recharge. Pervious concrete pavement is an alternative approach where interconnected voids in the concrete allow water to flow through the pavement structure. This study investigates the possibility of pervious concrete pavement to improve infiltration and to contribute to the recharge of the phreatic zone. The main difference between pervious concrete and conventional concrete is the open-graded aggregate structure and limited or no use of fine aggregate. Thus, this network of interconnected pores provides a conduit for water movement through the pavement. Previous experimental studies have shown that the hydraulic performance of pervious concrete is greatly influenced by aggregate size, cement content, water-to-cement ratio, compaction, and void content. Field investigation of pervious concrete pavement in Ahmedabad indicated successful drainage and evaluated its strength, void ratio, permeability, and infiltration performance. The proposed method treats the pavement, granular sub-base, and underlying soil as an integrated infiltration system. Field studies of two-layer pervious concrete pavement systems have shown water infiltration through both the pervious concrete and the granular sub-base. Therefore, selecting the right pavement mix and sub-base is important to achieve sufficient permeability without sacrificing the required structural performance. The proposed system has the potential to reduce surface runoff, improve stormwater management, and provide an opportunity for groundwater recharge where site conditions permit.

papers.title: Field-Scale Demonstration of Model-Free Reservoir Characterization and Rapid Production Forecasting Using Physics-Informed Machine Learning
papers.source: SPE Annual Technical Conference and Exhibition
papers.summary: Abstract Building geological models from diverse field data may require considerable multidisciplinary effort depending on the reservoir and decision complexity. Furthermore, dynamic model calibration for production forecasting using historical data typically necessitates numerous full-physics simulations in traditional history matching workflows, often leading to prohibitive computational cost for field-scale applications. Purely data-driven machine learning (ML) models can bypass high-fidelity model construction by learning statistical correlations between measured inputs and forecast targets and enable production forecasting. However, such models require extensive training data, lack physical interpretability and mostly exhibit limited predictive capability. To address these limitations, we propose a physics-informed ML framework for reservoir characterization and production forecasting based on observed well data without the need to construct high-resolution reservoir models. The proposed physics-informed neural network (PINN) is built on a reduced physics model in which each well is modeled as a single node with associated pore volume and transmissibilities for each injector-producer pair. The inputs to the network are observed operational responses, including water injection rates and bottomhole pressures and the network predicts nodal pressures and phase saturations as outputs. Phase-wise production rates are subsequently computed using calibrated physical parameters inferred by the network. The ML loss function combines data misfit terms with a physics-based regularization term defined as the node-wise material-balance residual derived from the conservation equations. During training, both the neural network parameters and physical parameters are calibrated, including nodal pore volumes, inter-well transmissibilities, well indices and relative permeability functions. papers.title: MF6PQC v1.0: coupling MODFLOW 6 and PhreeqcRM for variable-density reactive transport with evolving porosity and hydraulic conductivity
papers.summary: Abstract. Geochemical reactions can alter groundwater flow by changing solution density and porous-medium properties. Representing these feedbacks requires consistent exchange of chemical states and physical properties between reaction, flow, and transport calculations. We present MF6PQC v1.0, a Python framework coupling groundwater flow and transport in MODFLOW 6 with geochemical reactions in PhreeqcRM. MF6PQC updates solution density and converts mineral-volume changes into changes in porosity, hydraulic conductivity, and diffusion coefficients. It supports three schemes for coupling transport and reactions while retaining existing flow and geochemical model-building workflows. Comparisons with two established reactive transport models showed agreement in component transport, mineral reactions, and the evolution of porous-medium properties. An idealized evaporating salt-lake model reproduced density-driven circulation and evaporite zonation. In a heterogeneous evaporite-leaching aquifer, dissolution concentrated flow along preferential pathways, and density feedback strengthened this redistribution. MF6PQC provides configurable coupling schemes and property relationships for examining these interactions in groundwater reactive transport.

Quantitative assessment of heterogeneity-controlled remaining hydrocarbon distribution in a mature sandstone reservoir using a detailed three-dimensional reservoir simulation model
papers.source: Journal of Petroleum Exploration and Production Technology
papers.summary: Abstract Accurate estimation of remaining hydrocarbon resources in mature reservoirs is strongly affected by spatial reservoir heterogeneity, which can limit sweep efficiency and create poorly drained compartments. This study quantitatively evaluates the influence of reservoir heterogeneity on the distribution and accessibility of remaining hydrocarbons in a mature sandstone reservoir of the Marib–Al Jawf Basin. A three-dimensional black-oil reservoir simulation model was developed by integrating geological, petrophysical, and historical production and pressure data. The model incorporates spatial variations in porosity, permeability, and fluid saturation across multiple stratigraphic units and was calibrated through history matching to reproduce field production performance. The calibrated model was then used to analyze heterogeneity patterns and identify poorly swept reservoir zones. Simulation results reveal pronounced lateral and vertical heterogeneity characterized by strong permeability contrasts that control fluid flow behavior, generate preferential flow pathways, and create isolated compartments with limited connectivity. Consequently, approximately 35–45% of the original oil in place (OOIP) remains trapped within poorly connected reservoir compartments despite long-term production. The results demonstrate that spatial heterogeneity is the dominant control on the accessibility of remaining hydrocarbons and that pressure maintenance alone cannot ensure efficient reservoir sweep. Unlike previous studies that primarily focused on production optimization, this study integrates quantitative heterogeneity analysis with a calibrated three-dimensional reservoir simulation model to identify poorly drained hydrocarbon compartments, providing a transferable workflow for resource assessment and future development of mature heterogeneous reservoirs.

Warm-sector heavy rainfall over the eastern China plains: identification, characteristics, and precursor dynamic signals
papers.summary: Abstract. Warm-sector heavy rainfall (WSHR) features small spatial scales, posing critical forecast challenges, while its fractional contribution to regional heavy rainfall and its short-term precursors remain poorly quantified. Drawing on 2021–2025 warm-season (June–September) observations from 493 surface rain gauges, ERA5 reanalysis, and a radar wind profiler (RWP) mesonet across the eastern China plains, we build an objective identification framework integrating automated front detection, warm-sector mask, and station-specific 99th-percentile hourly rainfall thresholds to separate WSHR from other heavy rain events. We detect 477 station-based WSHR events alongside 6002 non-warm-sector heavy rainfall events. WSHR exhibits scattered spatial distribution, peaks in July–August, and preferentially occurs overnight, with rainfall onset concentrated 2000–0300 Beijing Time. Accounting for merely 5–10 % of annual heavy rainfall occurrences, WSHR has shorter durations yet comparable median rainfall accumulations and heavier extreme rainfall tails. On average, they contributed 13.8 % of the total heavy-rainfall accumulation, and locally 40–50 %. Composite ERA5 fields show that WSHR initiates within an 850-hPa moist tongue of high pseudo-equivalent potential temperature south of the front, superimposed on strengthening low-level moisture flux convergence. RWP composites based on 62 WSHR events reveal a characteristically low and strong low-level jet that becomes increasingly frequent before the onset of rainfall, accompanied by enhanced kinetic energy and shallow vertical shear below 3 km and an abrupt ascent increase centered at 1–2 km within the final hour. These kinematic signals from wind profilers offer valuable observational precursors for predicting localized WSHR across the eastern China plains.

papers.summary: The NE Scottish coast between Portgower and Navidale contains an unusual succession of interbedded boulder beds and fine-grained rocks of upper Kimmeridgian to Tithonian (Upper Jurassic) age that have attracted attention for over 150 years. Their juxtaposition next to the Helmsdale Fault has commonly led to the inference that their deposition is entirely fault controlled and shows no systematic ordering. This study presents: the first centimetre-scale reproducible graphic log of this c. 4.3 Ma (610 m) sedimentary succession; new palynomorph biostratigraphy; detailed facies analysis; sketch maps; new ammonite finds and drone footage. Fine Assessment of Water Abundance and Water Inflow Potential in Coal-Bearing Strata Based on Water Storage Space Microelements

Groundwater in coal-bearing strata serves as the direct water-filling source for coal mining, and its water abundance significantly impacts the intensity of the mine water inflow. The coal-bearing strata in the Ordos Basin, China, were formed during the Jurassic period, and the coal measure sandstones are characterized by short diagenetic times, weak cementation, and significant variations in the water abundance. This paper analyzes the paleosedimentary environmental characteristics of the coal-bearing strata in the study area, revealing the distribution of sedimentary facies and their water-controlling rules. Utilizing fractal theory, the coal-bearing strata were three-dimensionally discretized to obtain water storage space microelements. By statistically analyzing the proportions of sandstones with varying grain sizes within the microelements and integrating porosity characteristics, the comprehensive water storage space of the microelements was derived. Finally, based on the sandstone water storage microelements, a three-dimensional evaluation of water abundance and an assessment of water inflow potential in the coal-bearing strata were conducted. papers.title: Debris Flow Dynamics in a Coastal Arid Catchment: Rainfall Thresholds and Numerical Simulation During the 2023 Yaku Event, Peru
papers.summary: Debris flows pose a significant hazard in mountainous and coastal arid regions, yet their rapid post-event assessment remains challenging. In March 2023, the Yaku event generated extreme rainfall across Peru’s Pacific watershed, triggering a hyperconcentrated flow in the Cusipata catchment, Lima department, Peru. This study presents an integrated analysis combining morphometric classification, hydrological modelling, and numerical simulation to characterise the hyperconcentrated flow hazard and support risk assessment. The catchment was classified as debris flood-dominated using three independent morphometric approaches, consistent with a hyperconcentrated flow regime inferred from field-measured sediment concentration. A local rainfall intensity–duration threshold was derived using a method based on Linear Regression-True Skill Statistic, providing a basis for early warning systems and validated operationally during the 2026 rainy season. The catchment hydrological response was simulated using event-based modelling, and the resulting hydrograph was used as input to RAMMS debris flow simulations with a Voellmy friction model. Two scenarios were evaluated: the Yaku event using the pre-event topography, and a post-Yaku scenario reflecting damaged retention infrastructure. Hazard maps indicate a significantly increased flow extent and intensity in the post-Yaku scenario due to compromised protective structures. These results were applied to support a formal risk assessment and demonstrate the value of integrating drone-derived topography, locally calibrated thresholds, and physically based modelling for post-disaster hazard characterisation in arid Andean catchments.

Dominant Disaster Mechanisms and Multi-Stage Mitigation of Debris Flows in the Eastern Qinghai–Tibet Plateau: A Case Study of the “8·03” Debris Flow in Ridi Gully
papers.summary: Debris flows in alpine canyon regions pose serious threats to infrastructure and human settlements due to their abrupt onset and high mobility, yet the interactions among topographic complexity, sediment supply, and mitigation performance remain insufficiently understood. This study integrates field investigations, hydro-meteorological analysis, and dynamic numerical simulations to investigate the “8·03” event in Ridi Gully, eastern Qinghai–Tibet Plateau. The results indicate that the initiation and subsequent evolution of the debris flow were jointly controlled by intense localized rainfall, abundant unconsolidated sediment, and steep channel gradients, with local blockage-breaching processes further amplifying flow velocity and impact energy. Mitigation simulations further show that the single slit-dam configuration reduced the debris flow deposition volume and area by 14.29% and 16.23%, respectively, whereas the combined slit-dam/rigid-check-dam configuration achieved reductions of 65.54% and 44.97% relative to the no-protection scenario. These results highlight the potential contribution of temporary blockage-breaching to downstream hazard amplification and demonstrate the different regulating effects of the tested mitigation configurations on flow intensity and sediment deposition. The findings provide case-specific insights into debris flow hazard evolution and staged structural mitigation in alpine mountainous environments.

papers.title: Efficacy of Negative Pressure Suction‐Assisted Flexible Ureteroscopy for Upper Urinary Tract Calculi and Construction of a Stone‐Free Rate Prediction Model
papers.source: The Kaohsiung Journal of Medical Sciences
papers.summary: This study retrospectively analyzed 92 patients who underwent negative-pressure suction sheath-assisted flexible ureteroscopic lithotripsy (observation group) and 85 patients who underwent conventional flexible ureteroscopic lithotripsy (control group). Propensity score full matching and weighted analyses were used to balance covariates. Operative time, hospital stay, pain scores, hemoglobin changes, white blood cell counts, neutrophil counts, stone clearance rates, and complications were compared, and predictive models for stone clearance were constructed. The observation group achieved significantly higher stone-free rates at 3 days (69.6% vs. 29.7%, p < 0.001) and 1 month (75.0% vs. 34.2%, p < 0.001) postoperatively. Relative to the control group, the observation group had postoperative white blood cell counts closer to normal values (9.25 ± 3.26 vs. 10.08 ± 3.78, p < 0.05), with a smaller increase from baseline (0.82 ± 4.90 vs. 2.96 ± 5.02, p < 0.05). The neutrophil percentage was also lower (0.73 ± 0.10 vs. 0.77 ± 0.07, p < 0.05), and visual analogue scale pain score was significantly reduced (2.00 ± 0.53 vs. 2.56 ± 0.89, p < 0.001). The predictive models achieved areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.727 (95% confidence interval: 0.616-0.839) at 3 days and 0.742 (95% confidence interval: 0.630-0.855) at 1 month postoperatively, indicating good discriminatory ability. This study shows that flexible negative-pressure suction sheath-assisted flexible ureteroscopic lithotripsy improves short- and mid-term stone clearance rates in patients with upper urinary tract stones. The models perform well and may facilitate individualized clinical decision-making.

papers.title: Disentangling the depositional, tectonic and diagenetic history of a unique case of rhombic calcite in marine carbonate scree‐like deposits in the Cretaceous Cauvery Basin
papers.summary: Abstract The Cretaceous Cauvery Basin along the eastern margin of India is associated with strong plume and rift‐controlled tectonic activity, causing highly variable sediment successions under fast relative sea level changes. The ~60 m thick fossil‐rich Kallankurichchi Formation comprises dominantly calcarenites, whereas its basal part contains mixed siliciclastic‐carbonate scree‐like conglomerates and dark grey limestone in the deepest section, possibly the result of a complex tectonic history. Due to the flow transformation, the clast‐supported scree‐like conglomerates grade into matrix‐supported debris flow conglomerates. One unit of these matrix‐supported debris flow conglomerates contains 6–14 μm sized calcite rhombs, which have not been previously reported for such deposits. Through integrated petrographic, geochemical and sedimentological analyses, we document the calcite rhomb formation and discuss their origin by either dedolomitisation or by meteoric diagenesis in shallow marine environments that were temporally subaerially exposed. The absence of any evaporites, absence of large quantities of originally high Mg components and absence of dolomite relicts limits the interpretation of dedolomite. Bored limestone clasts in the matrix‐supported debris flow conglomerates, and the occurrence of fully marine species such as Inoceramus is generally interpreted as scree‐like deposits in nearshore environments being deposited in fully marine conditions. papers.title: Quantifying Pore-Throat Heterogeneity in Bioclastic Limestones Using Multifractal Analysis: Insights from the Upper Cretaceous Khasib Formation
papers.summary: Abstract The heterogeneity of carbonate reservoirs constitutes a critical control on fluid flow. Nevertheless, most previous studies rely on qualitative characterization and single-scale statistical methods, which hinder multiscale characterization of pore heterogeneity and localized preferential flow. Furthermore, few quantitative studies have systematically clarified the coupled mechanism of deposition, diagenesis, and reservoir heterogeneity. To tackle this problem, this study targets bioclastic limestones of the Upper Cretaceous Khasib Member from Oilfield B in the Middle East. papers.summary: This paper presents new integrated micropaleontological data from two outcrops (the Agia Marina section) of the Kathikas Formation in southwestern Cyprus. Microfossil assemblages from pelagic interbeds within debris flow deposits are documented, including planktic foraminifera, benthic foraminifera, calcareous nannofossils and ostracodes. The biostratigraphic framework is primarily based on planktic foraminifera and calibrated with calcareous nannofossils zonations. Outcrop 21–32 contains a late Maastrichtian assemblage characterized by planktic foraminifera of the Abathomphalus mayaroensis Zone and calcareous nannofossils of the CC25c/UC20b Zone, consistent with previous age interpretations. Outcrop 21–31 yields microfossil associations including taxa indicative of the early Danian planktic foraminifera P1a Zone and the calcareous nannofossil NP1/CP1 Zone. The documented assemblages indicate that pelagic interbeds within the Kathikas Formation span the late Maastrichtian–early Danian interval. These results highlight the need to revise and extend the stratigraphic range of the formation. The new micropaleontological data indicate that deposition of the Kathikas Formation was contemporaneous with pelagic carbonates of the lower part of Lefkara Formation. Accordingly, the final stage of development of the Mamonia – Troodos nappe system occurred immediately prior to, or during, the late Maastrichtian.

Active earth pressure in unsaturated marginal backfills with stochastic tension cracks governed by the influence zone and transitional regime
papers.summary: Active earth pressure acting on retaining walls can be significantly affected by tension cracks that develop within unsaturated marginal backfills. Existing analytical approaches typically idealize these cracks as a continuous zone of uniform depth, neglecting their stochastic nature and the resulting variability in active thrust. This study presents a physics-informed stochastic framework for evaluating active thrust in unsaturated backfills containing spatially variable tension cracks. A physically admissible random field is developed in which crack depth is characterized by its mean, coefficient of variation, and correlation length, while crack location is governed by mean crack spacing. The generated crack field is integrated into a limit-equilibrium formulation incorporating suction stress and a log-spiral failure mechanism. Deterministic analyses first identify an Influence Zone (IZ) along the backfill surface where tension cracks affect active thrust. Monte Carlo simulations are then performed to quantify the influence of crack variability on the 95th percentile of the active earth pressure coefficient, K a,0.95 . Results reveal the existence of a Transitional Regime Domain (TRD) within the IZ where active thrust exhibits maximum sensitivity to crack variability and cracking-zone extent. The location and extent of the TRD depend on the statistical characteristics of the crack field, particularly mean crack spacing and depth variability. Among the stochastic parameters considered, the coefficient of variation of crack depth exerts the strongest influence on K a,0.95 , whereas correlation length has a comparatively minor effect over the conditions and autocorrelation models investigated. The proposed framework provides a practical tool for probabilistic assessment and risk-informed design of retaining walls with unsaturated cracked backfills.

papers.summary: Measurement of unsaturated soil hydraulic conductivity K ( h ), remains one of the most expensive and time-consuming procedures in geotechnical and hydrological engineering. This study presents a machine learning (ML) framework coupled with an interactive graphical user interface (GUI) for estimating unsaturated soil hydraulic properties from basic soil characterization data. The framework employs Random Forest and XGBoost ensemble algorithms to predict van Genuchten parameters ( θ r , θ s , α , n , K sat ) using readily available soil properties, including texture, bulk density, organic carbon, and particle size distribution. The models were trained and validated on a literature-derived synthetic dataset of 1500 soil samples generated using established empirical relationships from the ROSETTA, UNSODA, and Cosby databases. A 75/25 train-test split was used, with five-fold cross-validation performed on the training subset for hyperparameter optimization. Test-set performance yielded R 2 . Five-fold cross-validation yielded R 2 values of 0.766 for θ r , 0.937 for θ s , 0.995 for α , 0.984 for n , and 0.151 for log( K sat ). The predicted parameters were subsequently used to generate full Soil Water Retention Curves (SWRC) and unsaturated hydraulic conductivity curves K ( h ) via the Mualem-van Genuchten model. Comparison with classical empirical pedotransfer functions and multiple linear regression demonstrated comparable performance for K sat prediction while offering superior capabilities for full-curve generation. It is explicitly acknowledged that the reported accuracy reflects the models’ ability to reproduce synthetic reference targets rather than independent experimental observations. The accompanying interactive GUI enables real-time prediction, batch processing, and export of results for both research and practical applications in agriculture and environmental engineering.

papers.title: Radiocarbon in dissolved inorganic carbon in unsaturated zone soil water of semi-arid western India
papers.summary: Abstract Estimating groundwater age is vital for water management, especially in semi-arid regions, where aquifers are the primary freshwater source. Radiocarbon ( 14 C) dating of dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) is widely used to estimate groundwater age, assuming DIC is derived mainly from modern soil CO 2 , while soil carbonate contributions are considered 14 C-dead. However, in semi-arid regions, soil carbonates contributing to DIC in unsaturated zone soil water (UZSW) may contain measurable 14 C activity. This can impart an apparent age which is different from that assumed in conventional correction models and thus needs to be properly accounted for in groundwater age estimations. Here, we measured 14 C and δ 13 C in DIC in UZSW, soil CO 2 , soil carbonates, and soil organic matter to identify DIC sources and assess their impact on groundwater dating. Results show that the ages of DIC in UZSW range from 90 to 2290 years, with an average of ∼1240 years in semi-arid western India. We estimated that ∼13% of DIC derives from soil carbonates with 14 C ages in the range of 3500–14,000 BP in this region. These findings suggest that 14 C-based groundwater age estimates, particularly for groundwater younger than 10,000 years, may be biased if the 14 C activity of soil carbonates are not adequately accounted for. Our study also highlights the analytical challenges associated with isolating DIC for 14 C measurements. Overall, our results underscore the importance of characterizing the 14 C signature of soil carbonates and incorporating it into groundwater dating frameworks to improve the reliability of groundwater age determinations.

Diffusion analysis revealed that the diffusion coefficient increased from 5.0 × 10⁻10 m2 s-1 at 10 °C to 2.0 × 10⁻9 m2 s-1 at 50 °C, indicating that the ammonium diffusivity increases rapidly with temperature. Moreover, the hydraulic conductivity of the sand increased with both temperature and ammonium concentration, with the permeability increasing slightly from 1.46 × 10⁻6 m s-1 at 10 °C to 1.63 × 10⁻6 m s-1 at 50 °C. The simulations confirmed that the relationship between temperature and break-through behavior is nonmonotonic, reflecting coupled physicochemical transport and the competing influences of advection, diffusion, and adsorption processes. These findings highlight the urgent need for technical and management solutions to minimize environmental risks.

papers.title: Nonlocal interactions through hydrodynamics drive biofilm development and microbial competition in porous media
papers.summary: Abstract Microorganisms predominantly exist within soil-like environments as sessile communities called biofilms, where fluid dynamics critically shape their development and dispersal. Despite their central role in diverse systems, from biogeochemical processes to industrial filtration, oil recovery, groundwater contamination, and carbon sequestration, the mechanisms underlying biofilm-flow interactions in porous media remain poorly understood. Here, we combine microfluidic experiments with mathematical modeling to demonstrate that nonlocal interactions through hydrodynamic effects mediate intricate spatiotemporal dynamics and drive exploitative competition within porous media. Our results show that biofilms self-organize into clusters of biologically clogged channels interspersed with preferential flow paths (PFPs). PFP formation and stability result from feedbacks between local changes in hydraulic conductivity and global reorganization of flow patterns and pressure distribution. We reveal that PFPs tend to be unstable, with detachment of biofilm triggered when pressure differentials exceed critical thresholds. Based on simulations of competing populations, we suggest that these large-scale detachment events could be interpreted as an evolutionary trade-off, whereby bacterial matrices are sufficiently robust to withstand continuous shear stress while remaining sensitive to pressure-induced failure, thereby enabling nutrient access and avoiding redirection of resources toward competitors. The nonlocal nature of these hydrodynamic interactions shows that fitness in porous media must be thought of as a multiscale concept and provides new insights into bacterial adaptation strategies in porous environments. These findings further suggest targeted approaches for biofilm control in both natural and engineered systems.

papers.summary: Abstract Separated analyses are widely used to evaluate the stability of slopes after rainfall and earthquakes. However, the combined impact of rainfall infiltration and earthquake shaking on slope stability remains insufficiently studied. Therefore, a unique closed-form analytical solution to calculate the factor of safety (FS) for homogeneous unsaturated slopes under combined seepage and seismic forces has been proposed by modifying the conventional Bishop’s method. The two-dimensional seepage pattern was considered to capture rainfall infiltration, while pseudo-dynamic forces at each failure slice accounted for earthquake shaking. Further, an analytical search method was developed to locate the critical slip surface. Additionally, a coupled hydromechanical finite-element model was used to analyze rainfall-induced seepage, deformation, and stress redistribution. The resulting slope condition was further evaluated under seismic loading to represent rainfall–earthquake effects without implying full two-way coupling between infiltration and earthquake shaking. All these newly proposed methodologies were applied to the 2014 Malin landslide in Maharashtra, India, to replicate the landslide mechanism and identify root causes to show the application of proposed analytical solutions. A comparison with field observations and literature demonstrated that both the analytical and numerical models realistically represented the Malin landslide. Further, the proposed analytical model was validated against a numerical analysis of a real earthquake-induced landslide. The models accurately reproduced the onset, failure zone, and progression of instability over time. The present study provides the application of new analytical solutions for practical landslides, additionally offering a reference for prevention and evacuation plans.

papers.summary: Abstract Rheological parameters (e.g., pore pressure coefficient r u and dynamic friction angle ϕ ) are necessary input for landslide runout evaluation. However, due to high randomness of initiation, propagation, and accumulation, it is impossible to directly measure rheological properties. This study proposes an optimization method for calibrating landslide rheological parameters based on random forest (RF) and Nondominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II (NSGA-II). Firstly, a dynamic numerical model of landslide is established using three-dimensional model DAN (DAN3D). Then, the lateral accumulation width and the longitudinal runout distance at different spatial locations across the deposit are integrated to calibrate the rheological parameters. Next, the NSGA-II algorithm is employed to obtain the Pareto solutions of rheological parameters by minimizing the prediction errors of lateral and longitudinal runout characteristics at each location. To avoid extensive repetitive DAN3D simulations within NSGA-II, RF-based surrogate models are established to estimate the lateral and longitudinal runout characteristics at different spatial locations. The final optimal rheological parameters are objectively selected from Pareto solutions by the entropy weight method (EWM). Finally, the proposed approaches are illustrated and validated using two landslides that occurred in Gansu Province, China. Results indicated that rheological parameters optimized by the proposed approaches not only can accurately characterize the endangered area of historical events, but also provide reasonable forward prediction of runout behavior of similar landslide events with desired accuracy. RF surrogate models can remove the computational burden within NSGA-II. Integrating both the lateral accumulation width and longitudinal runout distance into the calibration of rheological parameters can improve the prediction accuracy of landslide endangered area.

papers.summary: Abstract Landslide-generated waves occur when sliding masses impact the water surface, potentially posing significant hazards to nearby areas. This study utilizes the smoothed particle hydrodynamics–distributed contact discrete-element method (SPH-DCDEM) coupling module within DualSPHysics to simulate landslide-generated waves in reservoirs, where the SPH method models the fluid flow and the DCDEM method captures the dynamics of the granular landslide mass. The accuracy and effectiveness of the SPH-DCDEM method in simulating landslide-generated waves are validated using two physical model experiments of subaerial landslide-generated waves. Using a simplified representation of a reservoir bank deposit at the RuMei (RM) Hydropower Station in China, this study conducts an in-depth analysis elucidating the key parameters that control landslide-generated waves in reservoirs. It is found that landslide thickness and landslide entry velocity are the primary controlling factors for two-dimensional granular landslides. Empirical formulas for predicting the maximum wave height and maximum run-up height for the RongSong (RS) landslide deposit at the RM Hydropower Station are developed. The results highlight the potential for more concentrated energy and greater destructive power in landslide-generated waves in mountainous reservoirs compared to those in open water areas.

papers.summary: Abstract Landslide hazards along the Banihal–Ramban corridor of the Jammu–Srinagar National Highway (NH-44) represent a critical geoenvironmental challenge in Northwestern Himalaya, where active tectonics, fragile lithology, steep terrain, and increasing extreme precipitation interact with intensive infrastructure development. This technical note presents a focused analysis of flash floods and landslides of April 20, 2025, examining their triggering mechanisms, cascading geomorphic processes, and impacts on transportation infrastructure and settlements. Historical landslide records (1990–2025) and regional hydroclimatic observations are incorporated to contextualize the event within evolving patterns of hazard frequency and anthropogenic slope modification along the NH-44 corridor. The April 2025 disaster resulted from the localized high-intensity precipitation, which elevated pore-water pressures, reduced slope stability, and triggered multiple failures in structurally weakened rock formations. Results highlight a transition from isolated slope failures toward compound and cascading hazard scenarios involving flash floods, debris flows, and infrastructure disruption. The study underscores the increasing vulnerability of this strategic Himalayan lifeline. It emphasizes the need for geologically informed engineering design, improved drainage management, and integrated early warning strategies to enhance long-term resilience.

papers.summary: Abstract Reliable InSAR-based monitoring of ground deformation is often hindered by atmospheric disturbances and phase noise, particularly in regions with rugged topography and high vegetation cover. However, limited work has explored integrated phase filtering and atmospheric correction strategies in complex, landslide-prone terrains like Mizoram, India. This study proposes an enhanced methodology combining a Modified Goldstein phase filter and Atmospheric Phase Screen (APS) removal to improve Line of Sight (LOS) displacement estimation. Mizoram, characterized by frequent landslides and challenging climatic conditions, provides an ideal testbed to evaluate these improvements. Twenty Sentinel-1 SAR images (10 ascending, 10 descending) were processed using SRTM DEM-based co-registration, with corrections addressing height distortions and DEM voids. This study modifies the standard Goldstein filter that incorporates Local Incidence Angle (LIA) information to enhance phase unwrapping stability, combined with Atmospheric Phase Screen (APS) removal applied before phase filtering. Furthermore, an ensemble learning framework using a Random Forest regressor was employed to model and refine time-series displacement trends. The proposed method constrained phase values within a range of -3 to 3 radians, improved displacement map interpretability, and achieved a LOS displacement of±80 mm/month. Additionally, 5-fold cross-validation of the Random Forest ensemble model yielded training and testing R² values of 0.892 and 0.856, respectively, confirming the reliability of the displacement estimates.

papers.summary: Abstract Landslides are among the most destructive natural hazards, causing substantial loss of life and infrastructure, particularly in mountainous regions. This study evaluates kernel-based machine learning approaches, namely, kernel logistic regression (KLR) and support vector machine (SVM), for landslide susceptibility mapping (LSM) in Sikkim, India. Model performance was quantitatively assessed using accuracy, kappa coefficient, specificity, area under curve (AUC), landslide density, and success rate curve (SRC). Furthermore, the landslide density analysis showed a systematic increase in landslide concentration from low to high susceptibility classes for nonlinear models, while SRC results indicated moderate to good predictive capability across all models, confirming effective spatial prioritization of landslide-prone areas. Additionally, a feature importance analysis was conducted to identify the most significant factors influencing landslide occurrence.

papers.summary: Abstract Landslides are common geological disasters that cause extensive damage and significant harm. Efficient recognition of landslide remote sensing images holds both theoretical and practical importance. However, practical landslide detection faces challenges including limited data, high computation, large memory use, and low accuracy. In this study, high-quality landslide remote sensing images were collected from southeastern Xizang to construct a landslide remote sensing data set. To address the issue of insufficient samples, an improved model, landslide-deep convolutional generative adversarial network (L-DCGAN), based on DCGAN, was proposed to enhance landslide remote sensing data. The enhanced data set was constructed by incorporating efficient channel attention (ECA) and squeeze-and-excitation (SE) modules into the generator and discriminator, respectively. Additionally, an improved YOLOv8 model, landslide-you only look once version 8(L-YOLOv8), was proposed. First, the cross-stage partial pyramid convolution (CSPPC) and grouped and shuffled convolution (GSConv) modules replaced the cross stage partial layer with 2 branches (C2f) module and ordinary convolution in the network to reduce the number of model parameters and computational complexity. Then, the spatial and channel synergistic attention (SCSA) mechanism was introduced to improve detection accuracy. Experimental results showed that compared with the original YOLOv8 algorithm, the number of model parameters in L-YOLOv8 was reduced by approximately 41.78%, and the average accuracy on the landslide sample data set was increased by 0.57%, and frames per second (FPS) was improved by 33.87%. The model achieved lightweight design while improving detection speed and accuracy, and demonstrated superior performance on the landslide remote sensing data set.

papers.title: Analytical Solutions for Water Infiltration in an Infinite Vegetated Slope under Heavy Rainfall and Its Shallow Stability
papers.summary: Abstract Heavy rainfall is a common natural phenomenon. Regarding the issue of water infiltration in an infinite vegetated slope (consisting of rooted and unrooted layers) under the heavy rainfall condition, the infiltration process is divided into two stages— before and after the slope surface reaches saturation—and the corresponding analytical solutions are acquired through several mathematical approaches. Then the proposed solutions are effectively verified by two comparisons. Finally, based on the factor of safety ( F s ), the effects of key factors on the slope’s shallow stability are quantitatively investigated, and some novel findings are obtained. For example, an increased heavy rainfall rate reduces the F s , but this effect exhibits a tendency of increasing and then decreasing. An increase in transpiration rate enhances the infinite vegetated slope’s whole stability, while its influence will be declined after the heavy rainfall infiltration. The increased root tensile strength improves the F s within the rooted layer, but does not affect the unrooted layer’s stability. Moreover, compared with the “exponential” root shape, the F s within the unrooted layer is slightly lower in the case of the “uniform” root shape. Overall, the findings provide useful insights into infiltration mechanisms and shallow stability of infinite vegetated slopes under heavy rainfalls.

The bridge is a post-tensioned cast-in-place segmental cantilever structure featuring a box girder spanning 180 m. Situated on a slow-moving landslide, the bridge failed on August 20, 2023. Analyses indicated that the concrete crushing of the bottom slab of the 180-m-long box girder triggered the failure. The suction stress that contributes to the resistance of the soil mass governs the stability of geostructures and depends on the thermal and hydraulic interactions in unsaturated soil. No solutions are available to determine the suction stress in soils subjected to transient flow conditions at elevated temperatures. This study develops closed-form expressions for temperature-dependent suction stress under transient flow conditions using the one-dimensional transient flow equation and a temperature-dependent soil–water retention curve. The developed equation was implemented within the framework of stress-based finite-element limit analysis to evaluate the stability of strip plate anchors in terms of their uplift capacity embedded in unsaturated sand, silt, and clay under transient flow conditions and varying temperatures. The critical role of thermal and hydraulic interactions in different types of unsaturated soils (clay, silt, and sand), specifically regarding matric suction, effective degree of saturation, and suction stress over time, has been discussed in detail. Additionally, a comprehensive parametric study has been conducted to evaluate the effects of transient flow and elevated temperature on the uplift capacity of shallow strip plate anchors. The results indicate that the behavior of plate anchors in unsaturated sand and silt is distinctly different from that in clay.

papers.summary: Abstract The paper focuses on the effect of the vertical ground acceleration component on slope stability. The proposed stability method is based on Newmark’s sliding block concept, which provides an intuitive indicator of slope stability. Contrary to the original Newmark method, both components of excitations, tangent and normal to the slip plane, are considered in force equilibrium. In the paper, the extended Newmark method is coupled with dynamic response obtained using the FEM and a direct time-integration scheme. Coupling the simple stability approach with the stress distribution history eliminates uncertainty in determining the intensity of the dynamic load acting on the sliding block. In the coupled method, the equilibrium of the sliding and resisting forces is considered along the discretized slip plane. When the limit equilibrium is reached, the relative movement of the block begins, and the permanent displacement of a sliding mass is accumulated. The influence of excitation components on permanent displacement is examined using a uniform steep slope as an example. The presented results indicate that shallow deformation mechanisms are more strongly affected by inertial forces than deeper ones. In the analyzed cases, the peak average acceleration for the shallow mechanism was between 1.2 and 3.0 times that for the deep mechanism. Furthermore, the effect of vertical acceleration on permanent displacements is notably more significant in shallow failure modes. It is shown that the permanent displacement obtained by the original Newmark’s method can be 74.3% lower than that obtained by the extended Newmark’s method. The impact of vertical acceleration itself can reach 24.6%.

papers.summary: Abstract Landslides are among the most significant natural hazards in the Himalayan region of India, causing substantial damage to infrastructure, natural resources, and local communities. This study presents an integrated hydro-geotechnical approach for regional landslide susceptibility assessment by combining statistical susceptibility mapping with slope stability evaluation. The proposed framework considers the influence of key hydrologic factors, including rainfall, drainage density, topographic wetness, and groundwater conditions, together with geotechnical properties to better explain the mechanisms controlling slope failure. Five bivariate statistical models, namely, frequency ratio (FR), information value (IV), weight of evidence (WoE), certainty factor (CF), and Shannon entropy (SE), were applied to produce landslide susceptibility maps. Their performance was evaluated using the area under the curve (AUC) and landslide density index (LDI). Among the evaluated models, SE achieved the highest predictive accuracy ( AUC = 87.17 % ), followed closely by FR (87.06%). The results indicate that steep slopes ( > 30 ° ), weak lithological formations, high drainage density, and groundwater conditions are the main factors controlling landslide occurrence in the study area. Slope stability was further evaluated using laboratory-derived geotechnical parameters and circular failure charts (CFC), providing an independent assessment of slope conditions under different groundwater scenarios. The combined use of statistical modeling, hydrologic factors, and geotechnical verification improves the reliability of landslide susceptibility assessment and provides a practical framework that can be applied in other mountainous regions affected by rainfall-induced landslides.

papers.summary: In slope instability hazard assessment, it is essential to account for uncertainties associated with both soil heterogeneity (the mechanical and physical properties of the soil) and environmental conditions, such as hydraulic boundary conditions, external loads, and seismic actions. This study investigates the reliability of slope stability by integrating both the intrinsic and spatial variability of soil properties together with hydro-mechanical and seismic loading effects. Two representative case studies are analysed: a natural slope and a zoned earth dam. A combined deterministic–probabilistic framework is employed, in which the Bishop limit equilibrium method is used to calculate the factor of safety, while probabilistic methods including Monte Carlo simulation, the First-Order Reliability Method (FORM), and random field modeling, are applied to estimate the probability of failure. Sensitivity analyses are also conducted to identify the most influential parameters affecting slope stability. The results indicate that groundwater level rise, seismic acceleration, and soil heterogeneity significantly increase the probability of failure. Further more, kriging-based random field models demonstrate that spatial variability of soil shear strength parameters has a decisive effect on reliability estimates. The study demonstrates that neglecting either spatial variability or seismic loading leads to a misleading stability assessment, particularly for slopes and earth dams subjected to unfavourable hydrogeological conditions.

papers.summary: Landslide dams, formed when landslide debris blocks a river, occur across Aotearoa New Zealand. These events pose serious hazards to downstream communities and infrastructure, as sudden breaches can result in unexpected flooding and debris flows. They are also important components of complex cascading slope-river systems. Despite their contribution to sediment cascades and potential flood hazard, they remain under-researched. papers.summary: Rainfall-induced slope instability is one of the most critical geotechnical hazards worldwide, causing significant damage to infrastructure and loss of life. Predicting slope stability under rainfall conditions remains challenging due to the complex interaction between soil properties, slope geometry, and transient hydrological processes. This research addresses this challenge by developing a reliable and practical predictive framework that integrates experimental investigation, numerical modeling, and machine learning. The study was conducted in three sequential stages. First, geotechnical centrifuge tests were performed at the University of Western Ontario to investigate slope response under controlled rainfall conditions. A calibrated rainfall simulation system ensured uniform and repeatable rainfall application, while slope deformation and pore water pressures were monitored to understand failure mechanisms. Second, numerical simulations using SEEP/W and SLOPE/W were conducted to evaluate slope stability across a wide range of conditions, including different soil types (clay, silt, and sand), slope geometries, and rainfall scenarios. This process generated a comprehensive dataset of 21,438 cases. Finally, machine learning models, including Multiple Linear Regression, Random Forest, and Extra Trees, were developed to predict the factor of safety using seven input variables. The Extra Trees model showed the highest predictive accuracy and strong generalization capability, particularly under unseen slope geometries. The results also highlight the importance of including rainfall intensity and duration in predictive models. The developed model was implemented into a web-based early warning system capable of providing rapid predictions. This research contributes to improved hazard assessment and supports the development of practical tools for geotechnical risk mitigation.

papers.summary: Landslides are processes involving the downslope movement of soil and/or rock masses due to slope instability. Wonogiri Regency exhibits diverse topographic, rainfall, geological, land-use, and soil characteristics, resulting in varying levels of landslide susceptibility across the region. This study aims to analyze the spatial distribution of landslide susceptibility levels and their correspondence with actual landslide occurrences in Wonogiri Regency. A quantitative method was employed using a Geographic Information System (GIS) approach via the Weighted Overlay method. The parameters utilized included rainfall, slope gradient, geology, land use, and soil type. Each parameter was assigned a score and weight, followed by an overlay process to generate a landslide susceptibility map. Validation was conducted using 85 landslide occurrence points from 2025, obtained from the Wonogiri Regency Regional Disaster Management Agency (BPBD), with 12 of these points verified through field surveys. The results indicate that landslide susceptibility is categorized into four classes: low, moderate, high, and very high. The moderate susceptibility class covers the largest area. Validation results show that 57 occurrence points (67.06%) fall within the high susceptibility class, while 28 points (32.94%) fall within the moderate susceptibility class; no occurrence points were found in the low susceptibility class. These findings demonstrate that actual landslides occurred more frequently in areas classified as having high susceptibility compared to those with moderate susceptibility.

papers.summary: (English) The top layer of soil on a slope is highly dynamic, influenced by atmospheric forces and the presence of vegetation. Many numerical models often neglect the vegetation impact on soil performance. papers.summary: Background: Landslides are a natural disaster that often occurs in Indonesia, particularly in areas with steep slopes and high rainfall. Bonto Lojong Village in Uluere District, Bantaeng Regency, exhibits these characteristics, yet there is no landslide susceptibility map for the area. Aim: To map the level of landslide susceptibility in Bonto Lojong Village, Uluere District, Bantaeng Regency, as a basis for disaster mitigation. Conclusions: Landslide vulnerability mapping using the frequency ratio method can produce maps with a good level of accuracy (AUC = 0.80). papers.title: Assessment of sediment production, connectivity, and delivery in mountainous catchments under environmental changes. The role of shallow landslides in the Upper Llobregat Basin (Pre-Pyrenees, Catalonia)
papers.summary: (English) Soil erosion in mountainous landscapes is strongly influenced by shallow landslides, particularly during extreme precipitation events. Despite their geomorphic significance, quantitative soil erosion studies often prioritize fine sediment dynamics and agricultural land-use calibrations, thereby underrepresenting the complexity of landslide processes driven by intrinsic slope parameters and external triggering forces. This study examines sediment production and connectivity from shallow landslides under climate change and land-cover transitions. The primary objective aims to quantify sediment mobilization from slope instabilities to fluvial networks, focusing on the Saldes River Basin (102 km²) for model calibration and applying the results to the Upper Llobregat River Basin (504 km²). The quantification approach used a distributed, event-based method with the FSLAM landslide stability model. The model uses a random-walk framework and applies the Index of Connectivity (IC) to estimate sediment volume fluxes from source areas to channel networks. The input data includes a digital elevation model, IC maps, and sediment source maps derived from shallow landslides. The model outputs consist of raster maps that describe sediment flux. papers.title: A framework for spatio-temporal assessment of slope stability along mountainous transport corridors
papers.summary: Globally, research on the interaction between roads and landslides has largely focused on roads as triggering factors. papers.title: Analisis Tingkat Kerawanan Longsor Lahan Di Kecamatan Ile Ape Timur Kabupaten Lembata Provinsi Nusa Tenggara Timur (NTT)
papers.source: UMS Library Center of Academic Activities (Universitas Surakarta)
papers.summary: Landslides are a common natural disaster in areas with steep topography, including Ile Ape Timur Subdistrict, Lembata Regency, East Nusa Tenggara. This disaster is caused by a combination of natural factors, such as high rainfall, slope gradients, soil types, and human activities that alter land use. This study aims to analyze the landslide susceptibility levels and identify mitigation efforts in Ile Ape Timur Subdistrict. This research employed a descriptive method with a Geographic Information System (GIS) approach. The data used included slope gradient maps, soil type maps, rainfall data, and land use maps, analyzed using a weighted overlay technique to produce a landslide susceptibility map. Primary data were collected through field observations, while secondary data were obtained from relevant agencies such as BPBD and PUPR of Lembata Regency. The results show that the landslide susceptibility levels in Ile Ape Timur are categorized into four classes: not susceptible (3,174 hectares), less susceptible (25 hectares), susceptible (718 hectares), and highly susceptible (6 hectares). The main factors influencing susceptibility are steep slopes, Andosols soil prone to erosion, and relatively high annual rainfall. Recommended mitigation efforts include structural approaches, such as terracing and the installation of early warning systems (EWS), as well as non-structural approaches, including community education and disaster simulations. This study is expected to serve as a basis for the government and local communities to implement effective landslide disaster mitigation measures, minimizing material losses and casualties.

papers.summary: Vegetation has been used for slope stabilization for centuries, with conventional measures like soil nails and piles serving to complement the root reinforcement. It also reviews the state-of-the-art of existing methods for quantifying mechanical root reinforcement: theoretical models, experimental methods from laboratory to field-scale, and numerical approaches based on FEM and DEM. Building on identified gaps and the need for functional trait-based root classification, a three dimensional finite element model with an explicit representation of simplified roots is developed and validated against field scale direct shear tests on vegetated soil. A systematic parametric analysis quantifies the effects of RAR, geometric arrangement (radial vs. square), structural versus non structural root systems, and root orientation relative to the shear plane. The results show that RAR alone is insufficient to uniquely characterize mechanical root reinforcement, because root systems with the same RAR can mobilize substantially different strength increases depending on the presence of dominant structural roots, their orientation relative to the shear plane, and their spatial arrangement. papers.title: Development of an advanced computational approach for early warning and predictions of rainfall-induced slope failures
papers.summary: Rainfall-induced landslides are among the most common natural hazards, threatening lives, homes, and infrastructure worldwide. This research develops a novel approach to predict landslides and provide early warning, even when field data are limited. The study creates advanced computer models that represent real soil conditions and simulate how slopes respond to heavy rainfall. These physics-based models are then combined with machine learning that learn continuously from monitoring data, allowing predictions to be updated and refined over time. By improving prediction accuracy, this research supports more effective landslide early warning systems and helps reduce damage and loss of life.

papers.title: Analisis Spasial Kerawanan Longsor untuk Penentuan Titik Shelter di Kecamatan Petungkriyono Kabupaten Pekalongan
papers.source: UMS Library Center of Academic Activities (Universitas Surakarta)
papers.summary: Landslide susceptibility is a condition that indicates the level of potential for an area to experience landslides which is influenced by factors such as slope gradient, rainfall, soil type, geology, and land use. This study aims to analyze landslide susceptibility for determining shelter points in Petungkriyono District, Pekalongan Regency using a GIS (Geographic Information System)-based overlay method with ArcGIS 10.8 software. The data used include landslide occurrence data, DEMNAS Indonesia, RBI Indonesia, rainfall in 2014–2025, land use in 2025, distribution of disaster mitigation shelters, soil type, and geology of Petungkriyono District. The results of the study indicate that the level of landslide susceptibility in Petungkriyono District is dominated by high class with an area of 6930.5 Ha or 84.58%, medium class with an area of 1228.3 Ha or 14.99%, and low class with an area of 34.9 Ha or 0.43%. In general, every village in Petungkriyono District is characterized by high landslide vulnerability. Curugmuncar Village is the most vulnerable area, with a high vulnerability percentage reaching 96.68%. Disaster mitigation shelters are divided into four types: government, education, health, and worship shelters. There are three government shelters, 14 education shelters, one health shelter, and 27 worship shelters spread across all villages in Petungkriyono District.

papers.title: RAINFALL-INDUCED LANDSLIDE SUSCEPTIBILITY MODELLING FOR PREDICTION AND EARLY WARNING
papers.source: CINECA IRIS Institutional Research information system (University of Urbino)
papers.summary: Landslide detection and prediction rely on Digital Elevation Models (DEMs) as well as historical documentation of past events. Utilizing multiple elevation datasets and a landslide inventory, logical optimization methods to partition terrain into Slope Units (SUs) used as modelling units for landslide prediction is introduced. Landslide area, counts as well as terrain characteristics like homogeneous slope aspect are used and later unified into segmentation metrics to assess their performance in landslide susceptibility models. These terrain units are continued to be used in dynamic landslide susceptibility modelling through Generalized Additive Models (GAMs) to approach real-time landslide warnings for disaster and risk management. Particularly for rainfall-induced landslides, the integration of rainfall as a dynamic covariate in statistical modelling is approached. Keeping the selection of the mapping unit to SUs, first we utilize cumulative antecedent rainfall information by testing multiple time-windows to select the most-representative temporal bracket for the region. Secondly, while the first technique still remains using rainfall in a scalar form, we implement a functional GAM to utilize the time-series information and present rainfall as a temporally dynamic variable. The model performances undergo a number of validation techniques and the drawbacks of lacking information is explained with varying prediction power. These enhances in methodologies are presented to support Landslide Early Warning Systems (LEWS) for disaster risk and mitigation measures.

papers.title: Watershed-Scale Physics-Based Coupled Hydrological and Hillslope Stability Modeling of Rainfall-Induced Landslides: Back-Analysis and Forward Predictive Simulations
papers.summary: Severe storms can trigger hundreds to thousands of slope failures in mountainous regions. Predictive slope stability models play a key role in improving community resilience to this widespread hazard. However, several limitations still constrain the prediction of rainfall-induced landslides at a regional scale. Existing rainfall-induced landslide predictive models vary along three general modeling aspects: (a) predictive approach (empirical or mechanistic); (b) size of the modeled area (single hillslope to global-scale applications); and (c) prediction type (probabilistic or deterministic). For mechanistic models specifically, two additional aspects are relevant: (d) the hydrologic model (steady-state or transient conditions); and (e) the landslide failure mode (one-, two-, or three-dimensional). While numerous predictive models have been developed, most struggle to balance mechanistic rigor, predictive accuracy, and computational efficiency for regional-scale assessments. Many rely on simplified mechanistic assumptions, while others use empirical approaches that lack any physical basis. Even when more rigorous mechanistic models exist, high computational costs, limited scalability, and sensitivity to input availability and quality affect their performance. CRISIS integrates a pseudo-three-dimensional slope stability approach with a hydrological model selected by the user, here implemented with the Parallel Integrated Hydrologic Model (ParFlow). papers.title: The influence of the Critical Zone on hillslope hydrology and stability
papers.source: Institutional Research Information System (Università degli Studi di Trento)
papers.summary: The Earth's near-surface layer, which extends from the vegetation canopy to unweathered bedrock, is known as the Critical Zone (CZ). It is essential for regulating the incidence of hydrological processes and hydro-geo hazards. Enhancing predictive models of infiltration, discharge production, and landslide initiation, requires an understanding of the relationships between the CZ and hillslope hydrology. In this research, the impact of changes in CZ configuration and characteristics on hillslope hydrology and stability is examined in various geomorphological and climatic contexts. The research begins by investigating rainfall infiltration mechanisms in the stratified pyroclastic soil-mantled slopes of the Campania region, Southern Italy. Field monitoring, laboratory infiltration experiments, and physically based hydrological modeling were combined to reproduce observed pore-water pressures, soil-moisture dynamics, and subsurface flow mechanisms. The findings enhanced our understanding of rainfall-induced slope instability and provided further insights into the redistribution of water in layered volcanic deposits. The work expands by using a coupled hydro-mechanical framework to forecast the onset of shallow landslides. The framework combines i) a transient hydrological model with ii) a finite element solver for slope stability in order to iii) compute local field factors of safety (LFS) under dynamic rainfall conditions. The framework's ability to faithfully replicate observed hillslope failures is validated against a benchmark test and actual storm events in the Braies Alpine Catchment, Alto Adige, Northern Italy. This supports the framework's use as a large- scale, cost-effective tool for quantitative hazard assessment in mountainous regions. The focus then shifts to exploring how the internal structure of the CZ controls hydrological response and slope stability, using the Coos Bay experimental catchment CB1 in Oregon, USA, as a test case.
